harnesses.name: Refio
harnesses.notes: Headless Refio CLI, the system this benchmark exists to tune.

scores.rationale: All three modes exist: human vs human with WASD and arrows, CPU vs human, and CPU vs CPU. The CPU uses BFS to steer toward the food. The grid is 30x30, with wall and self collision, growth, scores shown during play, a start menu, a game over screen, and R to restart. Gaps: R only works after game over, not mid-game. The CPU snake does no trap avoidance. The brief asks for a snake game but the whole game is built around two snakes, so there is no single-player mode.

There are no console errors, the menu buttons work, the game loop runs, and the interaction shots show a game over screen appearing. Snake-to-snake collisions are handled for head-on and body hits. Minor bugs: head-on swap crossings can pass through each other unnoticed. When both snakes hit a wall in the same tick, P1 is always blamed. The snakes start only 3 cells from each other's path and collide quickly without input. On the game over screen, the leftover canvas snake segments and food show faintly through the overlay and look cluttered.

It is a clean dark theme with a styled menu, coloured scores, and a grid. It is acceptable but basic. The scoreboard is visible behind the menu and game over overlays. The overlay is semi-transparent, so leftover snake pieces and the food show through awkwardly. There is no animation, polish, or on-screen controls beyond a small hint.

The code is readable, with sections, comments, and sensible function names. The logic is simple and consistent. Weak points: inline onclick handlers, duplicated food-placement loops, and a BFS that copies whole paths at every step. The lightenColor helper has confusingly swapped variable names, though it works.

The code is split into config, state, core logic, input, AI, and rendering sections. There is clear duplication: two near-identical snake objects, mirrored key handling for the two players, and duplicated collision checks. The 'isCPU' flags are set after resetGame, and the game uses global mutable state. The result is acceptable but not tidy.

Movement, growth, wall and self collision, and snake-vs-snake collision work correctly. The BFS correctly avoids both bodies and finds the shortest path to the food. Reversing is prevented. Flaws: the BFS treats tails as obstacles even though they will move away. The CPU ignores where the opponent's head is likely to go. Its fallback when there is no path to the food is random with no space check, so it can trap itself. When both snakes die in the same tick, only the first is blamed. Head-swap crossings are not detected. The checks are sequential, so the loser is decided by check order.

Includes the 30×30 grid, wall/self and snake-to-snake collision handling, growth, scores, menu, game-over screen, restart key, two human control sets, and all three modes. CPU uses BFS to seek food. Restart by R only works after game over, which is a small gap in the restart requirement.

No console errors are reported, and the interaction shots show the menu click starts play, movement progresses, and collisions trigger game over. In the restart interaction, pressing R during active play does not reset the game; the timed shots remain on the static start menu, so they do not show gameplay progression.
The dark theme, colored snakes, score display, and menu are clear and consistent. The presentation is basic, with a large plain canvas and little visual detail beyond grid lines and simple buttons.

The code is readable, uses descriptive names, and separates input, AI, collision, and rendering logic. Some functions handle multiple responsibilities, and the BFS copies whole paths into its queue, which is inefficient.
Game state and core functions are organized into understandable sections, with limited duplication. The HTML uses inline event handlers, and utility and state logic remain in one large script.

Movement, growth, scoring, collision checks, and BFS food seeking are implemented. R only restarts after game over, and the BFS treats the snake's tail as blocked even when it will move away, which can cause avoidable detours or fallback moves.

All three modes exist: human vs human with WASD and arrows, CPU vs human, and CPU vs CPU. The CPU uses BFS to steer toward food. The grid is 30x30. Wall, self and snake-to-snake collisions are handled, and the start menu, game over screen and R restart are present. Two things hold it back. The 900px canvas is taller than the 800px viewport with overflow hidden, so the score row at the top of the board is clipped off-screen. R restarts only the same mode, with no way back to the menu. There is also no score summary on the game over screen.

There are no console errors, and the menu buttons, key input and game over flow all work. The main defect is that the 900px board is centred in an 800px viewport with overflow hidden. The top and bottom are cut off and the score display sits off-screen, so the score is not visible during play. In the screenshot the game over panel is also clipped. Both snakes start facing each other and end in a draw within seconds in human vs human. The CPU has no look-ahead, so it can trap itself.

It has a clean dark theme, a green title, hover buttons and distinct snake colours, with a subtle grid. It is basic: the head eyes are a placeholder dot and there is no responsive scaling. The canvas overflows the viewport and is clipped, which hides the score and the board edges. The game over panel is a translucent black box on a black canvas and looks flat.

The code is readable and commented, with a sensible split into init, loop, move, collision, AI and draw. It has weaknesses: BFS copies the path array on every node, and shifting the queue makes it O(n²). The fallback move shuffles with a biased sort. A comment in the draw code says eyes 'could go here', which marks unfinished polish. The CPU fallback is crude and has no flood-fill safety check.

The two snakes are duplicated global object literals, and init repeats the same fields for each. Game state is global and the menu buttons use inline onclick handlers. Functions are reasonably named and small. There is little dead code, but the unused 'eyes' placeholder remains. The CPU and human control paths are split across the loop and the key handler, which is acceptable.

The core logic is right: growth, wall and self collision, head-to-head draws, and body collisions between snakes. Direction buffering stops 180° reversals. Defects: the CPU treats its own tail as an obstacle, and it ignores the opponent's likely next move. It has no trap avoidance or longest-path fallback, so it can enclose itself. Food spawn loops forever if the board fills. A fast double key press between ticks can still reverse the snake, because the reversal check uses the current dx/dy rather than the buffered direction. The score is never shown on the game over screen.

The artifact includes a 30×30 grid, all three modes, food growth, wall and self collision, scoring, menus, and a CPU that uses BFS to seek food with collision avoidance. The visible score elements are absent from the rendered page, and the game-over flow does not show scores, so it falls short of complete score presentation.

The page runs without captured console errors, the start button works, gameplay advances, and R restarts. However, the score display is not visible, and the interaction shows both snakes dying in a draw after about 4.5 seconds despite only one snake receiving movement input, making the main two-player mode difficult to use.

The simple dark grid, contrasting snake colors, food, and centered menu are readable and consistent. The large fixed 900px canvas is clipped in the 800px viewport, and the score board is not visible, which keeps the presentation from feeling polished.

The code is readable, uses descriptive function names, and separates game logic from rendering. It has noticeable issues including an unbounded food-placement loop when the board is full and inaccurate game-over messaging when only one snake dies.

The single-file implementation is divided into configuration, state, game loop, AI, rendering, and input sections. State is held in duplicated global snake objects and several responsibilities are tightly coupled, and the two-snake scoring/rendering setup is incomplete.

Movement, growth, wall/self collisions, cross-snake body collisions, mode selection, and BFS food seeking are implemented. CPU pathfinding treats its own current body, including the tail that may move away, as blocked and does not account for simultaneous CPU movement; fallback steering can also leave the snake stationary if no safe move exists. These flaws undermine reliable play.

All three modes (human vs human, CPU vs human, CPU vs CPU) are present. The grid is 30x30. Walls, self-collision and snake-to-snake collisions end the game. Food makes the snake grow. Per-player scores show during play, and there is a start menu, a game over screen and restart with R. The CPU uses BFS toward the food. Gaps: restart only works from the game over screen and goes straight back into the same mode with no way back to the menu, and the CPU is plain BFS with no trap avoidance.

There are no console errors. The menu buttons and the 1/2/3 keys work, the game runs, and the game over screen appears with R to restart. Minor defects: any single death ends the whole round immediately, so the survivor never keeps playing. The human snake starts heading at the wall and dies quickly if the player does nothing. There is no pause.

The dark theme, green glow title and styled menu buttons are acceptable. The in-game scores are small and low-contrast. The 600px board is plain flat squares with no snake heads or eyes. The game over overlay is basic, so the look is functional rather than polished.

The code is readable and works. It carries leftover stream-of-consciousness comments in handleInput ('Wait, Mode 2 is CPU vs Human...'), a redundant GRID_SIZE constant, an empty if-block, and a mode 1/2 conditional that is confusing.

Functions are separated sensibly (spawnFood, moveSnake, checkCollisions, bfs). There is duplication: snake1 and snake2 are copy-pasted objects, and the wall, self and body collision code is duplicated per snake. Input handling has dead or muddled branches, and BFS copies the whole path array at every step.

BFS steers correctly toward the food and avoids walls and bodies. Flaws: CPU pathing ignores the tail moving away and the other snake's next move, and it picks a random move when no path exists. Head-on collisions are handled, but both snakes' bodies are checked after both have moved. Spawn food ignores a full board. Reversal prevention checks the current direction rather than the queued one, so two fast keypresses in one tick can reverse the snake into itself.

Includes the 30×30 grid, three modes, CPU food pathfinding, two human control sets, scoring, collision handling, menu, game over screen, and R restart. Two-snake collisions are handled. The CPU can still take traps, and food spawning can loop indefinitely if the board fills.

No console errors were captured, and the interactions reach gameplay and a game-over screen. However, the timed shots are inconsistent: the first two are blank and the third shows the menu. In the human-vs-human interaction, the default-moving first snake reaches a wall and ends the game within the wait, making play dependent on controlling both snakes promptly.

The dark arcade palette, glowing title and food, clear player colors, and centered game board form a cohesive presentation. The canvas is visually sparse during play, and the initial timed screenshots are blank.
The single-file implementation is readable and has no captured runtime errors, but comments include contradictory mode/control assumptions and the full-board food spawn case is not handled.

Game state, controls, movement, rendering, and pathfinding are separated into functions, but there are unused constants and repeated collision and movement logic. The BFS repeatedly copies full paths and performs linear queue removal.

The main movement, growth, scoring, wall/self collision, and snake-to-snake collision paths are implemented. CPU pathfinding avoids current occupied cells but does not plan for future body movement or trap avoidance; food spawning can become an infinite loop when no free cells remain.

All three modes exist: human vs human with WASD and arrows, CPU vs human, and CPU vs CPU. The CPU uses BFS toward the food, there is a start menu, a game over screen with scores, and Enter restarts. The grid is 20x20 (TILE_COUNT=20, 600px canvas), not the required 30x30; GRID_SIZE=30 is the pixel size of a cell, so the constant naming is misleading. Restart is Enter only, so the R key does nothing, and there is no way to return to the menu to change mode. Scores are shown, but not clearly labelled as CPU or human.

No console errors. The menu buttons start the game, and the loop runs and handles wall, self and snake-to-snake collisions, including head-on. The game over screen shows a winner and scores, and Enter restarts. Minor defects: the interaction shot shows a draw at 0-0 after about 4.5s because the snakes start 8 cells apart on a small grid, facing each other on the same row. Opposite keypresses such as ArrowRight for the blue snake are silently ignored. The score board has no per-mode labels.

Clean dark theme with a green title, readable menu buttons and distinct green and blue snakes. It is very plain overall. The board is smaller than a 30x30 grid would give, and the score board is hidden or dimmed behind the overlay. Snakes are plain squares with a barely lighter head, and there are no effects. Acceptable but not polished.

Readable and straightforward, with a single file and clear function names. The BFS builds a full path array per queue entry, which is inefficient. The misleading GRID_SIZE/TILE_COUNT naming and a comment that contradicts the 30x30 requirement stand out. The `keys` state is tracked but never used. lightenColor has swapped G and B variable names. Inline onclick handlers and global state are used throughout.

Reasonable function separation: reset, spawn, move, collisions, cpuMove, bfs, draw. Snake1 and snake2 are handled with duplicated code in collision checks and key handling. There is dead code: the unused keys map and keyup handler. The constants are confusingly named. Mode strings are magic literals, and the game-over logic has no shared player abstraction.

The main logic is sound. BFS steers toward the food and avoids walls and both bodies, with a fallback neighbour when no path exists, and reverse moves are blocked. Flaws: the grid is 20x20 rather than 30x30. The two CPUs plan simultaneously, and BFS treats tails as blocked. The fallback can choose a move that reverses direction, which is an instant self-collision. Only one input per tick is allowed through nextDir, so a fast double-key can still reverse the snake. Food spawning loops forever if the board fills. A head-on swap or collision is handled only partly. Collisions are checked after both snakes move, which is acceptable. The CPU has no trap or flood-fill avoidance.

All three modes, two human key sets, CPU food seeking, scoring, collision checks, a menu, game over screen, and Enter restart are present. The board is only 20×20 (600 px divided by 30 px), not the required 30×30.

The console error list is empty and the menu loads, but the interaction evidence shows the game immediately reaches a draw on the first click; the movement interaction also ends in a draw, leaving controls difficult to use. The timed screenshots are unchanged at the menu, so they provide no evidence of a running simulation.

The centered menu is readable and consistently styled, but the game and overlay are stark black with low-contrast score text, and the interaction screenshots show the game-over overlay immediately obscuring play.

The single-file implementation is readable and uses clear function names, but has logic and presentation defects, including the incorrect grid dimensions and controls that permit an immediate head-on loss.
Game state and behavior are separated into recognizable functions, though the two snake collision checks and controls are duplicated, and some state such as the key map is unused.

Food growth, wall and self collision, and CPU BFS food pathing are implemented. However, both snakes move and collide even in CPU vs Human mode, where snake 2 is not CPU-controlled; CPU pathfinding ignores the other snake’s planned movement, and the interaction evidence shows immediate simultaneous death in Human vs Human.

All three modes exist and the 30x30 grid is correct. Wall and self collision, growth on eating, live scores, a start menu, a game-over screen and R to restart are all present. The CPU uses BFS to steer toward food. Small gaps: no per-mode labels on the game-over screen, and the score board shows faintly behind the start menu. Nothing goes beyond the brief.

No console errors. The menu buttons start the game, the game runs, and the game-over screen shows after a collision. Snake-to-snake collisions are handled, including head-to-head. Minor defects: the game ends as soon as either snake dies, and the snakes start facing each other on the same row, so human vs human often ends in a quick draw (interact-2 shows a draw at about 4.5s). The CPU is not tuned for fair play.

A clean dark theme with a centred canvas, a decent menu, colour-coded P1/P2 scores and a glowing food block. It is basic: the food is a plain square, the snakes have no eyes or other detail, and the game-over panel does not match the canvas background. The scores show faintly behind the menu overlay. It is acceptable rather than polished.

Readable and organised into sections, but it has leftovers: an empty if-block in handleInput with 'Wait, logic check' comments, and a comment saying visual feedback for the selected mode 'could be added here'. The CPU fallback is a naive 'pick the first valid neighbour'. There is no shared tick rate for input. Several unfinished-looking comments.

Functions are separated sensibly (moveSnake, checkCollisions, cpuMove, bfs, draw), with two snake objects and a clear state machine. Dead code and stray comments remain, such as the empty if-block in handleInput. Collision checks are duplicated across snake1 and snake2. The BFS copies the path on every node and uses queue.shift(), which is inefficient. The player-to-controller mapping is hard-coded instead of configured.

The main path is correct: BFS to food with walls, own body and enemy body as obstacles; reversal is blocked; food does not spawn on snakes; collisions and the head-to-head case are handled. Flaws: the CPU treats the tail as blocked, does not anticipate the enemy's next head position, and has no trap or space-aware survival (the fallback takes the first free neighbour). The game ends when only one snake dies instead of letting the other continue. Both snakes move before collisions are checked, so head-swap passing is not detected.

Includes a 30×30 grid, three selectable modes, keyboard controls, food growth, wall/self and snake-to-snake collisions, scores, a start menu, game-over screen, and restart keys. The CPU uses BFS toward food, but excludes its own current body cells—including the tail that would vacate—so paths can be missed; the screen also mislabels CPU players as humans in game-over results.

No console errors were captured; the menu button starts play, the board advances, and R restarts after game over. In the recorded Human vs Human interaction, ArrowRight and ArrowDown led to a draw after about 4.5 seconds, so normal control play is short and the game-over result is abrupt; the CPU modes also have tail-blocking path issues.

The centered board, subtle grid, contrasting snake colors, and readable menus are clear and consistent. The presentation is plain, and the game-over screen gives generic player labels even in CPU modes.

The single-file implementation is readable and separated into game logic, input, AI, and rendering functions. Some misleading comments and leftover no-op mode logic reduce polish, and the BFS copies full paths as it searches.

Functions and state are named clearly and grouped by purpose, but collision, movement, mode handling, and UI updates are tightly coupled through globals; the redundant mode-check block and generic winner labels are unfinished details.

Core movement, growth, direction reversal prevention, wall/self collision, and simultaneous snake collision checks are implemented. CPU BFS treats every current body segment as a permanent obstacle, including the tail that may move away, and simultaneous movement can also make food spawning depend on move order; these flaws can cause avoidable misses and deaths.

All three modes, the 30x30 grid, scores, start menu, game over screen and an R key exist. But the CPU path-finding crashes (see logic_correctness), so the CPU snake never steers toward food in either CPU mode. The CPU mode, which is the core of the task, is therefore effectively missing. R also only returns to the menu instead of restarting directly.

There are no console errors on load, and Human vs Human starts and runs. Both snakes start facing each other on the same row, so a head-on draw is likely within seconds. The interact-2 screenshot shows a Draw game over with 0:0 score. CPU vs Human and CPU vs CPU throw a ReferenceError every tick, so the game freezes with no movement. A main feature is blocked. The 900px canvas is also cropped in an 800px-high viewport because the body has overflow hidden.

The dark theme, glowing title, bordered buttons and coloured P1/P2 scores are acceptable. The 900px board is clipped by the 800px viewport. The score board is hidden behind or cropped with the board. The game over overlay is plain, with the translucent overlay letting the snakes show through. There is no clear in-game controls hint and no polish beyond the basics.

The code is readable and commented, with sensible constants. It contains a fatal use-before-define bug in the BFS: `key` is a const used before its declaration. There is also an unused `hidden` fade transition, duplicated per-snake code, and leftover 'for now' comments.

Functions are separated sensibly into init, AI, update and draw. snake1 and snake2 are duplicated in their definitions, input handling, collision checks and drawing, instead of using an array of snakes. The `key` helper is defined in the wrong place. getNeighbors and isObstacle are reasonable. Global state is acceptable for one file.

In findPathBFS, `cameFrom.set(key(start), null)` runs before `const key` is initialised. This is a temporal-dead-zone ReferenceError, so every CPU move throws and the CPU logic never works. Even if that were fixed, isObstacle ignores the other snake's tail moving and has no trap or flood-fill check, and the fallback is random. The human-mode collision logic is sound: walls, self, head-to-head and head-to-body are all handled. Both snakes get the same food and the opposite-direction guard is present. The 180-degree guard uses dx and dy, so two quick key presses between ticks can still reverse the snake.

Includes a 30×30 board, all three modes, two control sets, food growth and scoring, wall/self/snake collisions, a start menu, game over screen, and R-key restart. The CPU uses BFS toward food with collision avoidance. It falls short of 5 because collision checks treat a moving tail as occupied, causing avoidable deaths, and the score only updates when food is eaten.

No console errors, the game starts and moves, and the screenshots show the snakes progressing. The interaction shows game over after the short control sequence, and restart returns to the menu. Collision handling can end a run prematurely because it counts tails that should vacate, and the 900px board is not responsive to the 1280×800 viewport.

The dark board, colored snakes, glowing food, and clear menu are coherent and readable. The fixed 900px canvas overflows the viewport, and the screenshots show no visible gameplay score during play, limiting the presentation.

The code is readable, uses descriptive names, and separates input, AI, update, and drawing logic. It has correctness defects in collision handling, and some comments describe features such as wall-distance preference that the fallback does not implement.

CSS, state, input, pathfinding, game updates, and rendering are organized into named functions. The implementation uses duplicated per-snake collision and drawing logic, and the BFS reconstructs its path by object identity, which works here only because it retains the exact start object.

The CPU searches for food with BFS, and the main movement, growth, scoring, and death paths are implemented. Collision checks include the current tail even when it will move, so a snake can die on a cell that should become free; the BFS obstacle check also ignores the tail while its actual collision check does not, making its planning inconsistent.

All three modes exist (two key sets, CPU vs Human, CPU vs CPU). The grid is 30x30. The CPU uses BFS toward the food. The start menu, game over screen, restart on R and Play Again button are all there. Defects: in the human modes the winner is never determined. Every wall or self crash calls endGame() with no winner, so the screen says "Draw!" even when one player clearly lost. The 900px container is taller than an 800px viewport and body has overflow hidden. The container is vertically centred, so the top and bottom are cropped, and the score bar at the top is likely off-screen. Pressing R on the start menu also starts a game.

There are no console errors, the menu buttons work, and the game runs. In the interaction shot with no steering, the two snakes start head-on on the same row and end in a "Draw!" within seconds. The game over text is wrong for most outcomes, because every non-head-on loss shows "Draw!". On an 800px-tall viewport the board and score are cropped. Snake-to-snake collisions are handled, but without a result. The Main Menu and Play Again buttons are stacked with no gap.

It has a neon green-on-black theme with glowing blocks and readable menu buttons, which is acceptable. The board is cropped by the viewport, and the score bar is hidden or cropped. The game over buttons touch each other. The overall design is minimal with little polish.

The code is readable and commented, and the CPU is a clear BFS. Snake state is duplicated as two near-identical object literals. The BFS copies whole paths in its queue. The game over winner logic is half-implemented. Inline onclick handlers and global state are used throughout.

Functions are sensibly split into input, loop, move, collision, CPU and draw, and names are clear. Defects: the snake definitions are duplicated. The input code repeats the same blocks for each player. getSafeMove duplicates collision logic. endGame takes an optional winner that is never passed for ordinary crashes. GRID_SIZE and TILE_COUNT are redundant.

Movement, growth, wall and self collision, and BFS food-seeking with obstacle avoidance all work. The tail is not popped before the collision check, so moving into the tail cell counts as a crash. The CPU has no trap avoidance or look-ahead, and its fallback just takes the first free neighbour. Winner determination is broken: crashing into a wall or itself yields no winner, so it always shows "Draw!". If both snakes die on the same tick, the first check ends the game with no handling. Pressing R on the menu starts a game in the stale mode.

Includes a 30×30 grid, all three modes, human controls, a food-seeking BFS CPU, scoring, collision endings, menus, and restart by R. Two-snake collisions are checked. The game-over winner message does not identify a player when a snake loses to a wall or itself, and the required filename is not evidenced.

No console errors; the screenshots show the menu, gameplay, movement after input, and restart working. However, the fixed 900px game area is clipped in the 1280×800 viewport, and games can end in a draw almost immediately when a snake hits the other snake, making play noticeably rough.

The neon palette and grid are consistent, but the black canvas and simple square sprites feel plain. The 900px board is clipped vertically in the screenshots, and score indicators are absent from the visible gameplay shots.
The single-file implementation is readable and has no runtime errors, but it relies on many mutable globals and inline event handlers. Collision and winner handling also have correctness gaps.

Functions separate input, movement, CPU routing, rendering, and game flow, but state is held in globals and collision rules are split across multiple routines. There is also no distinct scoring or end-game result for ordinary wall or self collisions.

The BFS CPU steers toward food, growth and wall/self collision checks are implemented, and snake-to-snake overlap is checked. However, collision checks happen after both snakes move and before tails are removed, so moving into a segment that would vacate that tick still counts as a collision. On non-head-on wall/self deaths, endGame receives no loser and commonly reports a draw rather than the surviving snake as winner.

The code has a start menu, a game over screen, three mode branches, BFS food-seeking for the CPU, a 30x30 grid, wall/self/snake collisions and a score display. But the menu buttons call `startGame()`, which doesn't exist (the function is `initGame`), so none of it can be reached. Other defects: human vs human has no separate key sets, because both humans share WASD and the arrows. Every mode spawns four snakes instead of two. Restart returns to the menu on any key rather than restarting the game.

console-errors.json shows 'ReferenceError: startGame is not defined' for each button click. The screenshots after clicking Human vs Human, pressing keys and waiting 4.5s still show the start menu. No mode can be started, so the game is unusable.

The dark theme, colored title and styled buttons are acceptable, but the menu is left-aligned inside the canvas and looks unbalanced. The gameplay visuals are never shown, because the game can't start. The design is plain.

The fatal mismatch between the inline `onclick="startGame(...)"` handlers and the actual `initGame` function means the code was never run end to end. There are also leftover redundancies (the `isPaused` flag is unused, and `showGameOver` has redundant status branches). The classes and BFS are otherwise readable.

There is a reasonable split into a Snake class, bfs, placeFood, init/draw/loop and UI functions, and the naming is clear. Against that: the dead `isPaused` flag, the redundant branches in `showGameOver`, the unused `p3IsCpu`/`p4IsCpu` plumbing, and the broken wiring between HTML and JS.

The BFS is a real shortest path to the food, so the CPU does seek it. But the game logic has major flaws. `bfs` compares `s.id !== selfBody[0].id`, and body segments have no id, so the CPU's own body is treated as an obstacle. Each mode spawns four snakes, so game over only fires when at most one is alive, and the unused pink and yellow snakes (P3/P4) run in every mode. Both humans share the same controls. Snakes are checked sequentially, so head-to-head collisions are resolved unfairly. Restart on any key goes back to the menu, not into a new game.

consoleErrors: ReferenceError: startGame is not defined

scores.rationale: The page shows three mode buttons, but each calls an undefined startGame function, so no mode can start. The CPU pathing also has a bug that makes it treat its own body as obstacles and fall back to random safe moves.
The captured console errors report ReferenceError: startGame is not defined, and the interaction screenshots show that clicking the mode button leaves the menu in place. The game never starts.
The centered game frame, dark palette, and clear buttons are coherent, but the visual treatment is basic and the nearly black canvas has little detail or contrast.
The code is divided into understandable sections and a Snake class, but the undefined startGame handler blocks the entire game, and the CPU pathing has a major obstacle bug.

The code has named game functions, a Snake class, and separate drawing and pathfinding logic. However, it includes unused state and CPU flags, repeats collision logic, and the missing startGame entry point leaves the structure incomplete.

The game cannot start because the buttons call an undefined function. In addition, the BFS obstacle logic compares snake IDs against selfBody[0].id, which is undefined, so it blocks the CPU snake's own body and causes random fallback movement; human input is also applied identically to every human-controlled snake.

consoleErrors: ReferenceError: startGame is not defined

scores.rationale: All three modes exist (human vs human, CPU vs human, CPU vs CPU). Human vs human uses WASD and the arrow keys. The grid is 30x30, with wall and self collision, growth, per-player scores, a start menu, a game over screen and restart on any key. The CPU snake uses BFS toward the food and avoids obstacles. Small gaps: restart is 'any key' and returns straight into the same mode, with no way back to the menu. The game ends as soon as either snake dies, and there are no extras.

console-errors.json shows 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading draw)'. The initial draw() call at load runs before snake1 and snake2 exist, so it throws a runtime error before any interaction, and the rules cap that at 0. The menu and game do work after a click. In interact-2 the game was already over within 4.5s, with P2 winning after hitting a wall.

The dark theme, coloured scores and styled menu buttons are acceptable. Defects: the menu buttons nearly overflow the 600px container, the canvas is blank before the first start, and the score bar sits outside the board. There is also a stray dim circle behind the menu and no polish beyond that.

The code is readable and sensibly commented, with a Snake class and BFS. Weaknesses: the initial draw() bug, BFS paths copied on every queue push, queue.shift() used as a queue, and inline onclick handlers with global state.

The code is split into config, Snake class, AI, loop and input, with reasonable naming. It has dead or duplicated code: getValidMoves is only a weak fallback, the BFS and move-validation obstacle building are duplicated, and the isCpu assignments in initGame are redundant. Snake.update reads the global snake1 and snake2 directly.

Reasonable function decomposition (BFS, tick, draw, init), but with dead code and duplication. initGame repeats near-identical snake setup three times, and the colour lookups are duplicated. All state sits in one IIFE.

Keys that don't belong to the active mode do nothing.

The HTML defines a cohesive dark game interface with a styled menu, scoreboard, game board, and game-over overlay. The header and menu text contain visible character-encoding corruption (replacement and control characters), which detracts from an otherwise polished presentation.

State, rendering, movement, and CPU pathfinding are separated into understandable functions, with little duplication. The unused `getHumanInputForSnake` helper, unused `lastTime` variable, redundant self-assignment, and input-handling inconsistencies keep it from a 5.

Human input routing omits WASD despite advertising it, and Arrow keys are not available to Player 2. If both snakes eat during the same tick, food is regenerated sequentially, so the second snake can score against the new food at its previous target.

All three modes, the 30x30 grid, a score display, a start menu, a game over screen and R to restart are present. Human vs human uses two key sets (arrows and WASD). scores.rationale: The page uses Canvas 2D and includes rotation, projection, culling, a moving light, keyboard handlers, and an FPS display. But it draws only one triangle per quad, assigns the same face lighting to all three vertices, and the interaction evidence reports no working elements.

The code is divided into named functions, but the central rendering logic has serious defects: lighting is identical at all triangle vertices, face colors are multiplied by 255 again, and each quad is only partly drawn.

The code has recognizable sections and descriptive function names, but includes unused face colors and a rasterizer that sorts vertices without using the sorted results; the per-face rendering is also duplicated only partially.

The pipeline has rotation and projection math, but it never shades individual vertices, omits the second triangle of each quad, and the lighting calculation treats the light position as a direction from the origin rather than from each vertex. These flaws prevent correct Gouraud shading.

The code has the pipeline pieces: vertices, rotation matrices, projection, a backface test and a scanline rasterizer. It never splits faces into triangles. Each quad is rasterized only as its first triangle (v0, v1, v2), so half of every face is missing. All three vertices of a face get the same colour from the face normal, so the shading is flat rather than Gouraud. Lambert lighting multiplies by 255 on top of 0-255 colours, so it clips to saturated flat colours. Perspective is wrong because FOV=500 is added to z. The light, W, P and FPS are present, but the core requirement fails.

There are no console errors, but the render is broken. The screenshots show huge flat magenta and green polygons that fill or overflow the canvas, not a cube. The perspective scale is almost constant, and the vertices are multiplied by WIDTH/2, so the cube is far too big. FPS reads 6-8 because the per-pixel fillRect with a fillStyle string is very slow. The page runs but is unusable.
The cube is not recognizable. Large flat saturated triangles are cropped by the canvas edge, with no visible shading gradient. Only the HUD styling is acceptable.

The code is readable and commented, but it has several real bugs: oversized scale, a missing second triangle, and a lighting multiplier that is applied twice. It is also very slow, recomputing the barycentric area per pixel and drawing with fillRect per pixel. The wireframe also draws all 12 edges, including hidden ones.

The functions are separated sensibly (rotation, projection, culling, lighting, rasterization, wireframe). Lighting is computed three times with identical arguments, and the unused rotationZ and normal-per-vertex setup are redundant. There are no per-vertex normals and no triangle-splitting step.

The logic has major flaws. Faces are not split into triangles, so the second half of each quad is never drawn. Vertex lighting uses the face normal, so it is flat. The lighting is scaled by 255 twice and saturates. Perspective uses FOV+z instead of a proper divide. Vertices are scaled by WIDTH/2, which makes the cube overflow the canvas. Backface culling uses the 3D-space cross product's xy components, not the projected ones, which is only valid under orthographic projection. The scanline edge intersection is fragile.

Rotation, projection, backface culling, and triangle rasterization are implemented, but lighting uses a single face normal and assigns identical colors to every vertex, so color interpolation cannot produce Gouraud shading. The code sets all three vertex colors of each triangle to the same face color (c0=c1=c2=col). The lighting is therefore flat per face, not per-vertex Lambert. The rasterizer has barycentric interpolation, but it interpolates identical colors, so there is no real Gouraud shading. Backface culling uses the wrong sign for the winding. The visible faces are culled and the inward-facing far faces are drawn. The moving light, W and P toggles, and FPS counter are present. Because of the flat shading and broken culling, the core requirement is not met.

The barycentric math itself is correct.

The Gouraud interpolation math itself is right.

All logic is packed into one large render() function. There is dead and duplicated code (drawTriangle versus the inline loop, unused tables and helpers). Colors are stored in a confusing 4-element [r,g,b,intensity] format that is later multiplied out. Naming is acceptable.

The barycentric test with no edge tolerance can leave cracks.

scores.rationale: Implements the 30×30 arena, food growth, wall and snake collisions, visible per-player scores, a start menu, game-over flow, restart key, and all three modes. CPU snakes use food-seeking BFS with collision avoidance. The AI does not fully plan for future traps, so it does not merit a 6.

The console error list is empty, the menu remains static as expected, and the interaction evidence shows the game starting, reacting to keys, and ending with a game-over screen. No runtime or interaction failures are evident.

The page is polished and cohesive, with clear score cards, a readable game board, strong contrast, and well-styled menu and game-over overlays. It is well beyond merely acceptable, though not exceptional enough for a 6.

The code is clearly named and organized into focused functions for movement, AI, collisions, rendering, and interface state. Some displayed separator characters are corrupted, but the code remains readable and the game runs.
Game state, mode configuration, UI elements, and core behaviors are separated cleanly, with little apparent duplication or dead code. The AI path search is self-contained and understandable.

The main game logic handles growth, food placement, wall and body collisions, simultaneous moves, head-on collisions, and winner determination. CPU pathfinding avoids currently occupied cells and enemy threats, but it does not guarantee that a chosen route remains safe as the board changes.

All requirements are present. The grid is 30x30. Wall, self and snake-to-snake collisions end the game. Snakes grow when they eat, and both scores are shown. There is a start menu and a game-over screen, and R or Enter restarts. All three modes exist (human vs human on WASD and arrow keys, CPU vs human, CPU vs CPU). The CPU uses BFS to the food while avoiding blocked cells and enemy head threats, with a flood-fill fallback. Pause and Esc to menu are extras. It falls short of a 6 because nothing goes far beyond the brief, and the CPU does not check for traps along its food path.

There are no console errors, and Start Match works. Snake-to-snake collisions are handled, including head-on and head-swap. Restart by R works. The game loop is time-stepped and guarded against pauses and background tabs. In the interaction shot the human game ended quickly with P1 hitting a wall because nobody steered it, which is expected. Minor issues: the menu button sits partly below the first viewport, and the CPU can walk into traps when it follows a BFS path without checking that an escape remains. Any crash ends the whole round immediately rather than only the crashed snake.

It has a polished dark neon theme with coloured per-player score cards, a canvas with glow, rounded segments and eyes on the heads, and well-styled overlays for the menu, pause and game over. The layout is responsive and has a keyboard instructions panel. The start dialog is slightly cramped, with the hint cut off at the fold of the first viewport.

The code is clean and readable. It has small, focused helpers, consistent naming, short comments where they matter, and a shared-snapshot collision step. There is no dead code. It is a single file with a sensible split between CSS, HTML and JS.

Functions are well named and responsibilities are separated (AI, tick, draw, input, state). Constants and the mode table are data-driven. Weaknesses: global mutable state, and updateInterface rebuilds the controls text with innerHTML and repeats strings that already exist in the HTML. The player roles hard-code index 0 and 1. There is no major duplication.

Both moves are evaluated against one shared occupancy snapshot, with correct tail-vacating, growth, head-on and head-swap handling and a single pending-turn queue that blocks reversals. The AI tail-availability check and BFS with a threat set are sound. Flaws: the human turn queue allows only one turn per tick, which is acceptable. The CPU takes the shortest path to the food without checking for trapping, and falls back to flood fill only when no route exists. The first crash always ends the round, with no per-snake elimination. The 'hit a snake' reason is generic.

Implements the 30×30 grid, growth and wall/self collisions, visible per-player scores, menu, game-over flow, keypress restart, and all three modes. The CPU uses food-seeking BFS with collision avoidance. Minor gap: CPU planning treats bodies as static, so it can miss paths that open as tails move.

No console errors were captured; the start button and restart interaction work, and the timed screenshots show movement progressing. Two-snake collision handling is present. No significant runtime defect is evident in the supplied evidence.

The full page is cohesive and polished, with clear score cards, a readable mode menu, and a consistent color palette. Some displayed keyboard glyphs render as replacement characters in the source, though the screenshot’s footer appears readable.
The JavaScript is organized into named functions and clear state handling, with readable constants and no obvious unfinished sections. Some UI strings contain garbled character sequences.

State, rendering, input, collision, and CPU logic are separated into sensible functions. The CPU pathfinding and movement update are somewhat complex but remain understandable, with little apparent duplication or dead code.

Core movement, food growth, scoring, collisions, modes, and restart logic are handled correctly. CPU BFS uses a static snapshot of body occupancy and may not account for tails vacating cells; its fallback chooses a spacious move but cannot guarantee a safe route.

All three modes exist: human vs human (WASD and arrows), CPU vs human, and CPU vs CPU. The CPU uses BFS to the food, avoids the opponent's head-adjacent cells, and falls back to a flood-fill area heuristic. The grid is 30x30. Wall, self and snake collisions end the game. Food growth, per-player scores, a start menu, a game over screen, and restart with R or Enter are all present. Pause and Esc-to-menu are extras. It falls short of a 6 because nothing goes far beyond the brief, and there is no single-player mode.

There are no console errors, and the game loop, tick and overlays are well-formed. Clicking a mode button only selects the mode, so the interaction shots still show the menu until Start is pressed. That is by design, but it looks inert to a tester. The window blur handler auto-pauses the game. I did not see in-game screenshots, so I scored from the code. Two-snake collisions, head-on hits and head swaps are handled. Minor issues remain, such as a head-to-head tie producing a draw. Overall there is nothing that blocks play.

The dark theme is polished, with gradients, colored score cards for each player, a blurred-backdrop modal menu, a canvas with a glowing food item, and snakes with eyes. The layout is responsive and consistent. The menu and score cards look professional. It is not a 6 because it is a standard, well-executed arcade look with no standout flourish.

The code is clean and readable, with helper functions, a fixed-timestep accumulator, and input buffering (one pending direction per tick). It uses a consistent state machine (menu, playing, paused, over). It has no comments, and the CPU function is long, with a nested closure. Otherwise it is tidy.

The structure is sensible: constants, a mode table, small pure helpers, and separate functions for reset, spawn, CPU, tick, draw and input. Naming is clear and there is little duplication or dead code. The CPU logic could be split into smaller functions. All of it sits in one script scope with global state, which is acceptable for a single file.

The tick resolves both snakes simultaneously. It excludes the tail cell from the occupied set when the snake is not growing, and it handles head-on collisions and head swaps. Food spawns only on empty cells, and a full arena ends the round. Reversal is blocked with a pending-direction buffer. The CPU uses BFS to the food, avoids cells next to the opponent's head, and falls back to flood-fill. It does not check whether the path to the food leaves a trap, which is a minor gap. No flaws found otherwise.

Implements a 30×30 board, continuous movement, food growth, wall and self collisions, visible individual scores, a start menu, game over flow, restart by keypress, and all three requested modes. The CPU uses shortest-path search with collision avoidance. It meets the brief well, though the CPU does not plan around future traps.

No runtime errors were captured, and the menu and keyboard interactions respond. The animation and movement have visibly progressed by the timed and interaction shots. Two-snake collisions are handled. Minor edge cases remain in simultaneous collision handling: a snake may be declared dead because the other snake's head enters its body even when that other snake also crashes.

The full page is cohesive and polished, with clear score cards, a readable menu, strong contrast, and consistent neon styling. It is well presented, though not distinctive enough to merit the exceptional score.

The code is readable and uses descriptive names, small focused functions, and no external dependencies. Some embedded UI text contains visible replacement or control characters where separators appear, which detracts from the finish.

Game state, rendering, controls, CPU movement, and collision logic are separated into understandable functions. The single-file structure is appropriate to the request, though there is no further modular organization.

The CPU searches for food with breadth-first pathing, avoids currently occupied cells and predicted opponent head moves, and falls back to choosing open space. However, collision resolution marks a snake dead when it enters the other snake's body even if that opponent also dies during the same tick, which can produce an unfair winner instead of a draw. CPU planning also treats occupied cells as permanently blocked, so it can miss routes that would open as tails move.

All three modes exist: human vs human (WASD and arrows), CPU vs human and CPU vs CPU. The CPU runs a BFS toward the food, avoids cells the opponent head could reach, and falls back to flood-fill. The grid is 30x30. Wall and self collisions end the game, and snake-to-snake collisions are handled. Per-player scores are shown. The start menu, game over screen, and restart with R or Enter are all there. Pause, a speed selector, and a main menu are extras. It falls short of 6 because there are no high scores and no single-player mode.

The game also auto-pauses on window blur. I could not see gameplay screenshots, so I judged play from the code.

The neon theme is cohesive, with glowing snakes and food, colour-coded score cards, blurred overlays, a responsive layout, and a clear legend. It is polished. The menu overlay covers most of the board, and the page is fairly standard in layout.

The code is clean and readable, with small focused functions, a state machine, and consistent style. Some magic numbers remain, such as 600 hard-coded in draw and CELL in other places. The CPU function is dense.

Naming is clear and there is little duplication. Helpers are separated into pathing, tick, draw, and input. Everything is global state in a single script, which is acceptable for one file. There is no dead code.

The tick logic is correct. The occupied set excludes tail cells that are about to move. Growth is handled, food spawns only on free cells, and head-on and swap collisions are covered. The CPU's BFS avoids bodies and opponent threat cells and uses flood-fill as a fallback. It only checks reachability of the food rather than whether the move leads into a trap, which is a minor flaw.

Game state, controls, CPU steering, collision handling, and rendering are separated into named functions with little apparent duplication or dead code.

The CPU does not check that the path to the food leaves a safe escape area, so it can trap itself. The head-danger avoidance is only one step deep.

Neurons grow branching, curved, step-by-step axons with accent branches, and pulses travel along them and cascade into child branches. Synapse formation is broken. The same branch tip pairs re-create synapses every 6 frames, which produces thousands of duplicates. Synapses carry no pulses. There is no stable-size stop for synapses, so the network is not stable.

Every control is wired through params and read live: growth speed, curvature, split chance, depth, threshold, glow, pulse speed, frequency, brightness and the colors. Regenerate, Clear and Pause work. Neuron count and max branch length only apply at regeneration. The background color, and the branch and pulse colors, apply live.

There are Branch, Neuron and Pulse classes, plus separate checkSynapses, init, GUI and animate sections, but the requested setup/GUI/growth/synapse/pulse/render sections are not clearly delimited. Drawing and growth logic are mixed in animate. The dedupe code is dead and ineffective. The state stays globally mutable.

The duplicate-synapse check compares p1/p2 against live tip objects, but the stored points are spread copies, so it never matches. Synapses are therefore re-added endlessly, which is an unbounded memory and render cost. Finished branches keep generating synapses, and there is no total branch cap. Pulses do not use synapses. The growth and pulse-following logic itself is sound.

However, the visible cube is almost uniformly dark, so the required Gouraud shading is barely discernible, and the controls are not surfaced as working interactive elements in the interaction evidence.

There are no captured runtime errors, the cube visibly rotates across the timed shots, and FPS updates. The independent interaction steps report no working interactive element, so the controls were not exercised by the evidence and remain a usability defect.

The page is visually sparse: a small, very dark cube and light marker sit on a large black canvas, with only a tiny HUD. The shading is difficult to see and the overall presentation has clear visual defects.

The code is readable and uses named helpers for matrix math, lighting, projection, and rasterization. Minor issues include the unusual replacement characters in one comment and an inefficient per-triangle image-data read and write.

The implementation is organized into clear geometry, math, state, input, and rendering sections with little apparent dead code. The triangle rasterizer repeats full bounding-box image-data operations for every face triangle, which is an avoidable structural and performance weakness.

The core transform, projection, culling, and barycentric color interpolation logic is present. But the lighting uses one flat face normal for all four corners, rather than per-vertex normals, so the vertex intensities on each face are effectively the same and the result does not produce the intended smooth Gouraud shading.

The pipeline is real. It has a vertex list, Rz·Ry·Rx rotation matrices, perspective projection, backface culling, quads split into two triangles, per-vertex Lambert lighting with attenuation, and a barycentric per-pixel color-interpolating rasterizer. The light moves, W toggles wireframe, P pauses, and the FPS counter is live. Gaps: the Gouraud effect is barely visible. Each face is lit by its single face normal, so the lighting is not a smooth cube-wide gradient. The shaded result is very dark, so the main effect is hard to see. The interaction screenshots had no real steps, so the W and P controls were not exercised visually.

There are no console errors, the cube rotates between shots, and the FPS reads 60. However, the cube is rendered almost black in every shot, so shading and light movement are hard to perceive. The light marker is always drawn on top of the cube, even when the light is behind it. The rasterizer calls getImageData and putImageData per triangle, which is inefficient. The page also uses image-rendering:pixelated on the canvas.

The cube is a barely visible dark navy on a black background. Face-to-face contrast and the Gouraud gradient are almost invisible in the screenshots. The HUD is minimal and the page is plain. Wireframe mode uses a pleasant cyan, but the default view looks like a clear visual defect.

The code is clean and readable. It has clear comments, small helper functions, an IIFE with strict mode, and a sensible frame loop. Minor issues: it allocates objects and arrays every frame, and there is a per-triangle getImageData call.

The code is well separated into math helpers, geometry, the lit-color function, the rasterizer and the frame loop. The naming is good. Minor issues: the vertex-color function is hardcoded to 4 corners, the material constants are inline, and the unused `az` is always 0.

The math is mostly right: matrices, culling via the rotated normal, projection, and barycentric interpolation. Defects: the lighting uses the face normal instead of smoothed vertex normals, so the 'Gouraud' effect only varies through light distance and angle across a flat face. The rasterizer's `>= 0` test and bounding-box approach can leave cracks between triangles. The light marker ignores depth ordering. The attenuation and ambient settings leave the result very dark.

scores.rationale: The artifact uses Canvas 2D for a rotating cube with perspective projection, backface culling, per-vertex Lambert lighting, triangle color interpolation, a moving light, W/P controls, and a live FPS display. The lighting uses radial vertex normals rather than face normals, so the cube faces shade as if smoothly rounded.

The console error list is empty, the timed screenshots show the cube rotating, and the FPS display reports 60. The code implements both keyboard controls, though the interaction evidence reports no working interactive elements, so those controls are not confirmed by the screenshots.
The cube is clearly visible with interpolated color and a readable HUD, but the page is otherwise an empty black viewport, and the broad, dark shading makes the cube's form less legible.

The code is readable and commented, with separate vector helpers, projection, rasterization, and rendering steps. Recreating a full-canvas ImageData object on every frame is an avoidable performance cost.
The pipeline is divided into named helpers and a clear animation loop. Some state and rendering work could be organized more efficiently, particularly the full-frame buffer allocation in each blit.

The main rotation, projection, culling, lighting, and interpolation path is present. Lighting uses each vertex's position as its normal, and depth is linearly interpolated in screen space rather than perspective-correctly, which can produce inaccurate shading or depth results.

The code has the full pipeline the brief asks for: a vertex list, rotX/rotY rotation, perspective projection, backface culling, quads split into triangles, per-vertex Lambert lighting, and a custom per-pixel barycentric rasterizer that interpolates colour. It is Canvas 2D only, with an orbiting light, a W wireframe toggle, a P pause and a live FPS HUD. Defects: vertex normals are the normalized vertex positions rather than face normals, which gives smooth "sphere-like" lighting on a cube. Rotation is applied as separate function calls rather than as matrices.

There are no console errors. Shot-1 and shot-3 show the cube rotating at 60 FPS with the light changing. The interaction screenshots are generic and show no real keypress test, so W and P are verified from the code only. Minor bugs: the large face stays almost uniformly dark teal, close to ambient only, so the lighting looks weak. The cube is very large in the viewport. The framebuffer is reallocated every frame via createImageData.

The gradients on the cube faces are smooth and there are no visible seams. The scene is dim, with a large dark teal face that reads almost flat. The background is plain black. Styling is minimal: a small monospace HUD and no floor or other context. It is acceptable but not polished.

The code is readable and commented, and it runs. There are leftover rambling comments about camera direction and culling, an unused camDir and unused helpers (v3, vAdd, vScale, vLen use), and an unused 1x1 imageData. The inner t is shadowed in the loop `for (const t of triList)`. Per-frame allocation is wasteful (createImageData and many small arrays).

Sections are separated into vec helpers, geometry, projection, rasterizer and main loop, with sensible names. Everything is in one IIFE with one large frame() function. It contains dead code (camDir, the unused imageData and imgDataBuf, v3), a lighting closure rebuilt per triangle, and rotation functions that act on vectors instead of matrices.

The culling, projection and barycentric interpolation all work. Lighting uses normalize(vertex position) as the normal, which is not a correct per-face or cube normal, and this causes the odd dim shading. The depth test uses interpolated world z, which is not perspective-correct, though it is harmless for a convex cube. The inside test uses a sign-agnostic rule with no top-left fill rule. Painter's sort plus a z-buffer is redundant. Edge pixels are rounded to integers.
