judges.rationale: The approach is the same in every attempt: a single HTML file with a canvas, a two-snake 'Snake Battle' layout (P1 green on WASD, P2 blue on arrows), BFS pathfinding for the CPU snake, and HTML overlays for the start menu and game-over screen. All six screenshots show the same three-mode menu with the same dark theme and green title. I read the code for attempts 1 and 4 and judged the other four from their screenshots and grep counts, so the quality differences below are limited to what those sources show. Quality and details vary. Attempt 4 is the clearest defect: TILE_COUNT is 20 on a 600px canvas with 30px tiles, so the board is 20x20 instead of the required 30x30. Attempt 1 uses a correct 30x30 grid with 20px cells. Attempts 2 and 6 have a taller, larger board in their screenshots. The restart key also differs: attempt 1 uses R and only works after game over, attempt 4 uses Enter, and attempt 5 shows 'Press Enter to Start'. Attempt 3 adds number-key shortcuts to the menu. The score display differs too: it is shown over the menu in attempts 1 and 5, but hidden until play in attempt 4. Overall the design is consistent but the correctness and polish differ.

All six use the same basic approach: a dark, canvas-based two-snake battle with the three mode choices, separate player controls, scores, and BFS-style CPU pathfinding. Quality and presentation vary: attempts 1, 3–6 show a centered menu with stacked mode buttons, while attempt 2 uses a much larger, full-screen layout with horizontal buttons and its screenshot cuts off the board. The screenshots also differ in whether scores are visible on the start screen and in styling, so the approach is consistent but the results are not fully comparable.

All six attempts take the same approach and reach about the same quality. I confirmed this by grepping the code and viewing three screenshots (1, 3 and 5). I did not open attempts 2, 4 or 6's screenshots or read any attempt in full. Each is a single-file HTML game titled "Snake Duel". Each uses a setInterval game loop at 100–120 ms. Each has a start menu with the same three modes (Human vs Human, CPU vs Human, CPU vs CPU), with a P1/P2 score header and a game-over screen with restart keys. Controls match too: P1 uses WASD and P2 uses the arrow keys. The attempts differ only in cosmetics and small details. Attempts 1 and 5 share a dark navy and red theme, while attempt 3 is black with green buttons. Attempt 3 also lets P1 use the arrow keys. Restart keys vary between R, Space, Enter and any key. Tick speed varies slightly, and the CPU function names differ. There is no sign of broken or wildly different attempts.

All six use the same broad approach: a single HTML file with a canvas, two snakes, a menu with three modes, score display, and game over/restart handling. Quality varies in the mode and movement logic: attempt 01 wraps at the edges and marks both snakes CPU-controlled in CPU vs human; attempt 02 uses wall deaths and maps CPU vs human correctly; attempt 03 uses inconsistent mode names in its AI checks and keyboard handlers; attempts 04–06 use different AI and mode mappings. The shared structure is consistent, but key gameplay behavior is uneven.

The six attempts share a broad template: a single canvas, a 30x30 grid, and two snakes. Beyond that they diverge in structure, AI approach and quality. The code organization differs. Attempt 1 uses a Snake class with a nextDir pattern. Attempt 4 uses global arrays (snake1/snake2, dir1/dir2) with a keys map. Attempts 2, 3 and 6 are class- or object-based with different internals. The CPU logic also differs. Attempt 1 uses a naive axis-first chase. Attempt 4 uses a greedy |dx|>|dy| step with no safety check. Attempt 2 filters safe moves and sorts them by Manhattan distance. Attempt 3 has a runAI with a safety check. Attempt 6 uses |dx|>|dy|. Restart behaviour is inconsistent. Attempt 1 restarts the same mode on any key. Attempt 4 returns to the menu on any key. Attempt 2 says 'Press R or Space to Restart'. Attempts 3, 5 and 6 say 'Press any key'. Quality varies a lot. Attempt 1 has a fatal bug: segmentsCheck references an undefined `nextH`, which throws a ReferenceError in CPU modes. It also sets both snakes to CPU in cpu-human mode, so there is no human player. Attempt 4 handles collisions and growth differently and looks visually different (dark theme, scoreboard above the canvas). Attempts 2 and 3 have safe-move AI. The visuals, with different themes and layouts in the screenshots, vary as well. This is divergent output with uneven correctness, not a stable pattern.

All six attempts converge on the same basic design and structure: a canvas-based two-snake game with a start menu offering Human vs Human, CPU vs Human, and CPU vs CPU. Their screenshots show comparable menu screens, though the styling varies. The implementations diverge more substantially in code organization and AI handling: attempts 1–3 and 5–6 use different `Snake` classes or update/AI routines, while attempt 4 uses separate movement and AI functions. Attempt 4’s screenshot also appears to show the scoreboard and food behind the start menu, unlike the other attempts. This is a consistent overall approach with some variation in execution and presentation.

I read attempts 01, 03 and 05 in full and viewed their screenshots. I did not open 02, 04 or 06 or their screenshots. I only ran a keyword count on those three, and it showed similar feature coverage. All three I read share the same design: a single HTML file, a 30x30 canvas grid, and two competing snakes on one board. They use a setInterval game loop at 100-120ms, a start menu overlay with three mode options, and a game-over overlay. They show a live score for P1 and P2, and the CPU snake uses BFS pathfinding to the food with a fallback 'any safe neighbour' move when no path exists. Quality is comparable: all are complete and playable, with wall, self and other-snake collisions and a restart path. The differences are mostly cosmetic or in UI details. Colour themes differ, with neon green on black in 01, a navy and pink palette in 03, and a teal and red palette with snake eyes in 05. The controls are swapped (01 has P1 on arrows and P2 on WASD; 03 and 05 have P1 on WASD and P2 on arrows). Mode selection is direct buttons in 01 and 03, but select-then-Start in 05. Restart is R in 01 and 05, but any key in 03. Scoring is +1 in 01 and 05, but +10 in 03. Small logic differences exist, such as 01 resolving head-on collisions by food, but none is a broken-versus-working split. No attempt looks broken, so quality is consistent and the approach is the same.

All six attempts use the same broad approach: a single HTML file with a canvas snake arena, two snakes, mode selection, scores, and CPU pathfinding. But the implementations vary noticeably: attempts 1, 2, 4, and 6 start directly from three mode buttons, while attempt 5 adds a mode selector and separate Start Game button; attempt 3’s screenshot shows the score display while the start menu is open. Canvas sizes and visual designs also vary, and the CPU-vs-human mode assigns the CPU to different players across attempts. The shared structure is consistent, but these differences make the quality and behavior uneven.

All six attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with a menu overlay for the three modes, arrow keys for player 1 and WASD for player 2, and a game-over overlay. I judged this from the screenshots only and did not read the code or run the games. The start menu differs a lot between attempts. Attempts 1 and 2 use mode buttons with no separate start step. Attempts 3 and 6 use radio buttons plus a Start button. Attempts 4 and 5 use a dropdown plus a Start button. Attempts 2, 4 and 5 show the score above or below the board, in different layouts. Quality also varies. In attempts 4 and 5 the game-over overlay sits on top of the dimmed start menu, so the two screens overlap and the game-over text collides with the menu. Attempt 4 shows a Restart button. Attempt 5 says to press R. The other screenshots show clean menus. So the approach is consistent, but UI structure and polish vary between attempts.

The attempts share the same broad approach: standalone HTML games with a start menu, three modes, keyboard controls, and CPU movement, usually drawn on a canvas. Quality varies substantially. Screenshots 1, 3, and 6 show a clear start menu; 2 shows the menu over an already visible blank board, while 4 and 5 show the game-over screen on top of the start menu, with text difficult to read. The implementations also vary in structure—attempt 4 uses a DOM grid instead of a canvas—and in game logic, including different CPU strategies and collision handling. This is a recognizable common approach, but not comparable quality across attempts.

All six attempts use the same basic approach. Each is a single-file HTML/CSS/JS dark neon Snake game with a menu offering Human vs Human, CPU vs Human and CPU vs CPU. All use WASD for player 1 and the arrow keys for player 2. The screenshots show the same overall look, a two-player score header over a boxed 30x30 arena. I judged this from the screenshots (1, 2, 3, 5 and 6), file sizes and keyword counts. I did not read the code or run the games. Quality and UX details vary between attempts. File size ranges from about 17 KB (attempt 5) to about 32 KB (attempt 3). The start flow differs: attempt 1 has mode buttons plus a Start Game button and Enter to start, and attempt 3 starts with the 1/2/3 keys and has an extra Mode score slot. Attempt 5 also starts with the 1/2/3 keys, and attempts 2 and 6 use clickable cards or buttons. The menu layout also differs. Attempt 2's menu looks washed out and faded, with the score header dimmed behind the overlay. Attempt 3 has a misaligned header overlap. Attempt 6 is a modal card, mentions BFS pathfinding and uses a separate food colour for each snake. Attempt 5 has the simplest UI. So the approach is consistent but polish, features and layout quality are variable.

All six attempts use a broadly consistent canvas-based, two-snake game with a start menu, keyboard controls, three modes, score display, game-over handling, and CPU pathfinding. Quality and mechanics vary: attempts 1, 3, 4, and 5 use a shared food target, while 2 and 6 give each snake its own food; menu layouts and controls also differ, and attempt 2’s screenshot shows a nearly black screen with its menu barely visible. The common approach is recognizable, but these differences make the results uneven.

The approach is the same in all six attempts. Each is a single HTML file with a 30x30 canvas, a dark-themed topbar showing scores and mode, and menu and game-over overlays with three mode buttons. Two snakes start at the same kind of positions (about x=8 and x=21 on row 15). The attempts that use a game loop use requestAnimationFrame with a fixed-timestep accumulator; attempt 4 uses setInterval instead. Quality and details vary between attempts. (1) The restart key differs. Attempts 1 and 2 use Enter, and attempt 2's Enter returns to the menu instead of restarting. Attempts 3, 4, 5 and 6 use R. Attempt 1 also adds Esc for the menu and a Restart button. (2) The controls differ. In attempt 1, P1 uses arrows or WASD and P2 uses IJKL, but the arrow keys also drive P2, so the two players' controls overlap. Attempt 2 uses arrows or WASD for P1 and IJKL for P2. Attempt 3 uses arrows for P1 and WASD for P2. Attempt 6 uses its own enqueueDirection input queue. (3) CPU quality varies. Attempts 1, 3 and 4 use BFS pathfinding with fallbacks. Attempt 2 only uses greedy Manhattan-distance steering with no pathfinding, which is weaker, and the greedy CPU can trap itself. Attempt 3 falls back to a random safe move. (4) Collision and game-over rules differ. Attempt 1 ends the game when either snake dies. Attempt 3 ends it only when all humans are dead or both snakes are dead, and in cpu-vs-cpu it ends only when both die. (5) Rendering varies, for example fading tails in attempt 1 and a roundRect polyfill in attempt 3. The skeleton is consistent, but the CPU intelligence, the key bindings and the game-over and restart behaviour differ enough to make quality variable.

All six attempts use the same overall approach: a self-contained HTML file with a canvas-based 30×30 Snake game, a start menu offering all three modes, live scores, keyboard controls, CPU movement, and a game-over/restart flow. The layouts, colors, labels, and CPU pathfinding details vary, but the screenshots show comparably complete menus and the code in each attempt includes the core game features. None stands out as broken or substantially lower quality.

I read attempts 01 and 05 in full and their screenshots. For 02, 03, 04 and 06 I only grepped the menu markup and the grep counts. Judging the rest from that sample, the approach is the same in every attempt. Each is a single HTML file with a 600x600 canvas on a 30x30 grid and a dark UI with overlays. Each has a start menu with the three modes, BFS pathfinding to food for the CPU, a setInterval tick of about 120ms, and Enter/Space restart. The details differ between attempts, so quality varies. Attempt 01 has mode buttons, WASD for Snake 1 and arrows for Snake 2, and fixed-direction BFS. It handles ties, with the CPU as Snake 1 in cpu-vs-human. Game over returns to the menu on Enter or Space rather than restarting directly. Attempt 05 uses radio buttons plus a Start button, so the menu UI differs. It has a different control mapping (arrows for Player 1, WASD for Player 2). Its CPU falls back to random safe moves. Game over ends the match on the first collision and restarts the same mode directly, and it shows a status per snake. Attempt 04 has Restart and Return to Menu buttons on the game-over screen. Attempts 02, 03, 04 and 06 use button menus with different mode ids ('human-human', 'hvh' and so on). Menu UI, restart semantics, game-over and collision rules, CPU fallback behaviour and control mappings differ, so quality is not uniform. The overall architecture and feature coverage are consistent, which makes this a consistent approach with variable quality.

The attempts diverge in both structure and implementation: attempts 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 use different canvas-based designs and game logic, while attempt 2 uses a CSS grid of cells. They also vary in controls, CPU pathfinding, and restart behavior. For example, attempt 1 assigns WASD to Snake 1 and arrows to Snake 2, while attempt 6 assigns arrows to Player 1 and WASD to Player 2; attempt 4 uses a distinct single-player-oriented design. This is not a consistent approach across attempts.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a single HTML file with a canvas, a setInterval game loop, a 30x30 grid, a mode-select menu, WASD plus arrow keys, and a CPU that picks moves. They differ in quality, and a few also differ in structure. Attempt 1 is the most complete. It has a BFS pathfinding CPU, self-tail handling, and a menu with an any-key start and an any-key restart. Attempts 2, 5 and 6 are working but simpler: they use a greedy Manhattan-distance CPU, with some gaps. Attempt 6 can only restart in the same mode. Attempt 2 restarts only on Enter or Space. Attempt 3 is badly broken. startGame sets isCPU and then calls initGame, which recreates the snakes with isCPU false, so both CPU modes never run a CPU. It also reassigns `const snake1Alive` and `const snake2Alive`, which throws a TypeError whenever snakes collide. Attempt 4 has a growth bug: grow() pushes a duplicate tail segment on top of the normal pop-less move, so it effectively grows 2 cells per food (it also has no CPU-vs-CPU score display). Structure also varies: plain objects with globals (1, 2, 3), classes (4, 5), and separate snake1/direction1/score1 variables (6). Canvas size is 600px in some attempts and 900px in others, and the score UI placement differs. So the approach is consistent but quality varies a lot, from fully working with BFS to nearly non-functional CPU modes.

All six attempts use the same broad approach: a single-page canvas Snake game with a start menu offering Human vs Human, CPU vs Human, and CPU vs CPU, plus score display and keyboard controls. The screenshots show comparable neon-green styling for attempts 02–05, while 01 and 06 use noticeably different layouts and visual treatments. Quality also varies: attempt 01 has the three modes and two-player score display, while attempt 06’s screenshot shows only a single score and its implementation uses a different, simpler structure. The common approach is recognizable, but the presentation and completeness are inconsistent across attempts.

I compared the six screenshots and counted matching keywords in the files. I did not run the games or read the code in full. The approach looks the same across attempts: single-file HTML with a canvas of about 600x600 px, a dark theme, and three game modes picked from a start menu. The menu UI differs between attempts, and one has a visible layout bug. Attempts 1 and 2 show a centred title with three stacked mode buttons. Attempt 3 has a 'Select Mode' heading with stacked buttons, and its canvas sits near the top of the page. Attempt 4's overlay is misplaced, appearing in the top-left corner and offset from the canvas, with a 'Press Enter to Start' prompt. Attempt 5 lays the three buttons out in a row. Attempt 6 uses radio buttons plus a 'Start Game' button, and the score HUD shows through the menu. This is the same core design with variable polish, and attempt 4's broken overlay suggests a real quality gap. The data does not show a wholesale divergence in approach, so it is not 0.

All six use a broadly similar approach: a 30×30 canvas, two snakes, keyboard controls, a mode menu, score display, food, CPU movement, and a game-over overlay. Quality varies in concrete ways: attempt 04’s screenshot shows the menu and game board misaligned and partly off-screen; attempt 06 has a malformed CPU-vs-CPU mode value and wraps at the board edges despite requiring wall collisions; attempt 01’s restart key returns to the menu instead of restarting play. The shared structure is consistent, but those differences make the results variable in quality.

All six attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with a canvas 30x30 grid, a mode-select start menu with Human vs Human, CPU vs Human and CPU vs CPU buttons, a purple/blue gradient theme and a snake emoji title. They differ in UI structure and apparent polish. Attempts 1 and 6 show the menu as a modal overlay over a dimmed game board and score panel. Attempts 3 and 4 show a standalone menu card with no board; 3 has emoji-decorated buttons and 4 has plain gradient buttons. Attempt 6 draws the menu inside the canvas area. The control schemes also differ. Attempt 3 gives Player 2 IJKL or the numpad, while attempt 4 lists Arrow Keys for both players in Human vs Human, which looks like a key conflict. Restart is by SPACE in some attempts and by R after game over in others. File sizes range from about 16.6 KB to 21.6 KB, which suggests different amounts of polish. I read the screenshots for attempts 1, 3, 4 and 6 and only searched the source of all six; I did not check the CPU logic or play any of the games. Because of that, the quality spread is a judgement from the UI and controls rather than from confirmed bugs.

All six use a similar canvas-based, two-snake game with a mode menu, scores, and game-over UI, so the overall approach is consistent. Feature completeness and implementation quality vary: attempts 02 and 06 only update snake 2 with CPU pathfinding, leaving CPU-vs-CPU incomplete; attempts 01 and 05 include AI for both snakes, while 03 and 04 use different game-state and control implementations. Restart behavior also varies between reloading, returning to the menu, and keyboard handling. The shared structure is recognizable, but the attempts do not reach comparable completeness.

All six attempts use the same basic design. Each is a single HTML file with a 600x600 canvas (30x30 grid, 20px cells) and a two-snake game. Each has an overlay start menu with the three mode buttons, a score display and a game-over overlay. Most use BFS for the CPU, with P1 on WASD and P2 on the arrow keys. Quality and details vary noticeably, though.

- **Restart key:** Attempt 1 uses Space only. Attempts 2 and 3 use Space or Enter. Attempt 4 uses R (and its keydown handler needs checking when no game has started). Attempt 5 uses any key. Attempt 6 uses R, plus Esc for the menu.
- **CPU quality:** Attempts 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 use real BFS pathfinding. Attempt 6 uses greedy Manhattan-distance steering with no pathfinding, so it is much weaker.
- **Gameplay differences:** Attempt 6 also has different start positions (5,5 and 24,24) and two food items. It also adds growth of 2 per food and a different tick loop (requestAnimationFrame instead of setInterval).
- **Structure:** Attempts 1, 3, 5 and 6 use Snake classes, while 2 and 4 use plain objects and functions.
- **Correctness:** Attempt 3's keydown handler dereferences `snakes[0]` before any game starts. Attempt 2's game loop is also less careful about collisions than 1 and 3. In attempt 5, the winner is decided by score rather than survival, and head-on collisions aren't handled the way attempt 1 handles them. Attempt 4 applies moves in separate passes, so head-on and growth edge cases behave differently.
- **Polish:** Visual polish ranges from glow and gradient effects to plain squares.

The approach is consistent but quality and rule details vary, so I rate it 0.5.

All six attempts follow the same broad approach: a single HTML file with a canvas-based 30×30 two-snake game, the three requested modes, keyboard controls, CPU movement, and menu/game-over flows. Their quality is uneven in the screenshots: attempts 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 show clean, centered menus, while attempt 4 has a visibly misaligned title and uneven button layout. The implementations also vary in controls for restarting and presentation; attempt 6 additionally shows garbled question-mark symbols in its headings and buttons. This is a consistent overall approach with noticeable differences in polish.

All six attempts use the same approach. Each is a single HTML file with a canvas and a dark neon-green card UI titled "Snake Game" or "Snake Battle". Each has a mode-select menu with Human vs Human, CPU vs Human and CPU vs CPU, a game-over overlay, and a restart key. I only compared screenshots and keyword counts, and I did not run the games. Quality and details vary between attempts. Attempt 1 shows a score bar (Player 1/Player 2) on the menu screen, and the others don't. Attempt 3 adds a separate 'Start Game' button and a 'R or Enter' restart key. Attempts 2 and 6 say 'press any key' to restart, and attempt 5 gives no restart hint on the menu. Control hints differ: attempts 2 and 6 mention WASD, attempt 3 lists only the arrow keys, and attempt 5 lists only 'Arrow Keys: Move Snake'. The attempt 4 screenshot shows a 'Game Over!' modal over a dimmed screen with a 'Play Again' button, apparently with no game board visible. That suggests a possible instant game over or a different game state from the others, though I did not confirm it. Overall the structure is consistent but the feature details and probable polish differ.

All six attempts use the same broad approach: a single HTML file with a styled menu, a 30×30 canvas game, two snakes, scores, and CPU movement. Quality varies in mode handling and restart behavior. Attempts 02, 03, and 05 assign the CPU and human players distinctly in CPU vs Human mode; 01 and 04 make both snakes CPU controlled there, and 06 assigns the CPU to Player 2 instead of Player 1. Restart behavior also differs: 02 and 03 support a keypress restart, 06 sends the player back to the menu after game over, and others rely on a button. Attempt 04 also uses a different select-menu layout. The repeated structure is consistent, but these functional differences make quality variable.

The attempts share a core approach, but quality varies. All six use a 30x30 grid and a setInterval tick. Each has two snakes, a greedy Manhattan-distance CPU, and an overlay for the menu and game over. Quality differs a lot. Attempt 06 starts with leaked model reasoning prose ('We need to create a new file...'), so the HTML shows that text as raw content. Attempt 05 is buggy: its CPU snake's autoMove always moves via move(), which drops the grow step, and its initGame calls the Snake constructor with a wrong argument list. Attempt 01 is cleaner but minimal. It uses a canvas-drawn menu, a 1-cell starting snake, and 'press any key' to restart. Attempt 06 uses clickable HTML buttons and restarts with R. Attempt 05 uses a DOM grid with CSS, not a canvas. The menu style (key-based vs button-based), the restart key, the rendering (canvas vs DOM) and the correctness all vary. I did not open attempts 02–04 in full, so this rests on the full reads of 01, 05 and 06 plus grep matches across all six.

The attempts diverge in implementation and quality. Attempts 1–4 use canvas-based games, but attempt 2’s screenshot shows only a blank canvas and title, while 1 and 3 show a working-looking start menu. All six attempts use the same basic approach and the same page scaffold: a single HTML file with a Canvas 2D software rasterizer, a Vec3 class or object, hand-written rotation matrices, painter's-algorithm depth sorting, a per-pixel barycentric fill, W and P key handlers, and an FPS counter. Quality varies a lot between them, and I judged that from reading the code, not from the screenshots. Attempts 2 and 3 use a flat face normal per vertex, so the Gouraud result is close to flat shading. Attempt 3 uses a 3x3 matrix with a +5 offset in the projection. Attempt 2 is the cleanest pipeline. Attempt 1 has a hard-coded face-normal table that is not used for culling, and it culls by cross product with a camera direction that looks questionable. It also performs 12 per-triangle putImageData calls. Attempt 4 culls with a face-centre dot product and uses fillRect per pixel, which is very slow. It projects with `fov/v.z` and returns null for z<=0 on a cube centred at the origin, so about half of the geometry is dropped and the cube is likely broken. Attempt 5 uses a cube of size 100 and a perspective function that also rejects z<=0, with a tiny scale. It builds per-vertex light by summing Lambert terms over the faces that share each vertex (a valid smooth-normal approach), but a single green material with a yellow light dot makes it look different from the rest. Attempt 6 allocates a full-canvas ImageData per triangle and calls putImageData at (0,0), which overwrites earlier triangles with transparent pixels. Only the last triangle would stay visible, and the wireframe mode is a separate path. The attempts also differ in structure: Mat4 versus Matrix3, a class-based Cube versus plain functions, quads versus pre-split triangles, and the light's orbit and visibility. The approach is the same in all six attempts. Each one is a single-file Canvas 2D CPU pipeline. The cube has 8 vertices and 6 quad faces split into 2 triangles. Rotation is Rx·Ry·Rz, projection is a perspective divide, and faces are culled and painter-sorted. Normals are averaged per vertex, with Lambert lighting at the vertices, and a hand-written scanline Gouraud rasterizer fills the triangles. Each has a W/P keydown toggle, an FPS counter, a moving light and a dot showing the light. Quality and correctness differ between attempts in the following ways.

- **Rasterizer:** Attempts 1 and 6 draw each scanline with a per-line createLinearGradient, so colours only interpolate along a line. Attempts 3, 4 and 5 write per-scanline ImageData with putImageData. Attempt 2 reads and writes a bounding-box ImageData with a barycentric test per triangle, which is the heaviest and slowest.
- **Matrices:** Attempt 2 uses real 4x4 matrices with a view-space projection and FOV. The others use per-vertex rotX/rotY/rotZ functions or 3x3 matrices with a fixed focal length.
- **Backface culling:** Three methods are used. Attempts 2, 3 and 4 use a screen-space 2D cross product. Attempt 1 uses a 3D face normal against a fixed view vector. Attempts 5 and 6 compute a view direction from the face centre. Attempt 5 puts the camera at +Z while its projection places the cube at z+5, so its culling and sort convention look inconsistent with the projection.
- **Normals:** Attempts 1, 2, 4 and 5 average face normals per vertex. Attempts 3 and 6 use normalize(vertex position).
- **Lighting:** Attempts 2 and 5 use a point light. Attempts 1 and 6 use a directional or normalised light. Attempt 6's light dot is a fake 2D orbit and does not match the actual light.
- **Rasterizer bug:** Attempt 5's scanHalf has a left/right colour-swap stub that does nothing.
- **Other defects:** Attempt 6 mixes a camera at the origin with a +4 offset. Attempt 3's wireframe draws triangle diagonals. Attempt 6 uses fixed per-frame increments, so its speed depends on frame rate, while the others use dt.

Overall the approach is consistent, but correctness, shading fidelity, performance and polish vary noticeably from attempt to attempt. I read the code only and did not open the screenshots.

All six attempts take the same basic approach, but their quality varies noticeably. I read the code only and did not open the screenshots. Each one is a single HTML file with a software barycentric rasterizer that writes into ImageData. Each builds a cube from 8 vertices and 6 quads split into 12 triangles, culls back faces, and does Lambert lighting with a moving light. Each has W and P key handlers and an FPS readout. The differences are in how well the pieces work.

Quality differences:
- **Attempts 1, 2 and 3:** These are the cleanest. They light each vertex with its face normal and the light direction, giving real per-vertex Lambert shading, and they sort back to front.
- **Attempt 4:** The light direction `L` is normalised from the light position alone, not per vertex. All three vertex colours are therefore identical, so each face is flat-shaded and not Gouraud. It also calls `getImageData` and `putImageData` for every triangle, which is slow. It leaves dead code in the light setup, and its rotation and light speeds are tiny constants (0.010 and 0.020 per normalised frame).
- **Attempt 5:** It uses sphere-style vertex normals (`normalize(v)`) and a white light, so the colour comes only from the lighting and the faces are not distinct colours. It also stops rendering entirely while paused, so the HUD no longer updates.
- **Attempt 6:** It adds a z-buffer, which the other attempts do not have. Its face labels and index lists look inconsistent: the faces are labelled +X and -X, but their index sets don't match those labels. It then patches the normals with a sign flip, and the camera sits at z = -4. The result is a much higher risk of wrong culling or wrong faces.

Other variation:
- **Wireframe:** Attempts 2, 3 and 6 draw it as an overlay on the filled cube. Attempts 1, 4 and 5 replace the fill with lines. Attempt 3 draws only the 12 cube edges.
- **FPS display:** Attempts 2 and 6 draw it on the canvas, and the others use a DOM element.
- **Canvas setup:** Attempt 2 uses a fixed 800x600 canvas. Attempt 3 stretches the cube non-uniformly to the window aspect ratio. Several others use the full window, and only attempts 1 and 4 handle the device pixel ratio.

The overall pipeline is consistent, but correctness (true Gouraud or not, face colours, culling robustness) and polish differ enough that this is consistent approach with variable quality.

All six attempts use the same basic single-page approach and implement adding, completing, deleting, filtering, and localStorage persistence. Quality is broadly comparable, but the results vary: attempts 1, 2, and 5 use a dark design, while 3, 4, and 6 use a light design; the layouts and controls also differ. Several artifacts contain visibly corrupted symbols for checkbox and delete icons, and attempt 3 handles malformed saved data less safely than the others. These are variations within a consistent approach, rather than fundamentally different or randomly broken solutions.

The six attempts reach very different quality, and the renderings diverge. Every attempt uses the same broad stack: a single HTML file, a canvas, dat.gui with four folders, and three buttons. That is where the similarity ends. I judged mainly from the six screenshots and a count of key API calls. I did not read the full source.

- Attempt 1 appears to be broken or blank. Its screenshot shows only the dat.gui panel on an empty dark page, with no visible canvas or network.
- Attempt 2 shows a large teal-flooded canvas. The background glow is wrong, there are only a few straight lines, and the pause control is a checkbox.
- Attempt 3 shows a dark canvas with a grid. Its branches end in big magenta blobs, so the synapse rendering is visibly off. The canvas also appears offset from center.
- Attempt 4 shows a small, sparse network with GUI folders expanded. Its controls use raw camelCase labels such as neuronCount. It has a yellow circle marker, a clean dark background and a pause checkbox.
- Attempt 5 is the most polished. It shows a well-formed branching tree with a blue glow, labelled controls and a proper vignette.
- Attempt 6 shows an oversized olive or yellow vignette ring that distorts the background. It has only a few short arcs, and its buttons are labelled "regenerate", "clear" and "toggle".

The attempts also differ in GUI labels, background treatment, and button and toggle style. Overall they range from a blank page to a well-formed tree, so the results look random rather than consistently good or bad.

The attempts use several different simulation structures, and their behavior varies sharply. Attempts 1 and 5 grow recursive branch trees, attempt 2 uses moving tips and stored line segments, and attempt 3 uses a separate step-based tree but never calls init(), leaving the canvas without a network; its GUI buttons also call init() only when clicked. Attempts 4 and 6 define branching logic that returns once a branch reaches full length, so branches never split. Attempt 5 adds a branch cap, while attempt 1 lacks one and repeatedly rebuilds synapses from every sampled branch point. The shared palette and dat.gui folders do not make their approaches or quality consistent.

The attempts diverge a lot in how they render and in how well they work. Judged from the screenshots alone; I could not run the shell commands to read the code. Attempts 2 and 5 show only a black screen, with the HUD but no cube (FPS 0 in attempt 2). Attempt 1 shows a purple cube that looks broken, with a stray, disconnected polygon and 17 FPS. Attempt 3 shows a flat-shaded purple cube with visibly uniform faces, so the Gouraud gradient is missing. Attempt 4 shows a dim olive quad plus a stray red line and does not look like a cube. Colour schemes, HUD layouts and FPS differ from one attempt to the next (17, 0, 39, 60, 60 and 17). All six attempts use a similar self-contained Canvas 2D pipeline with cube geometry, rotation, perspective projection, animated lighting, FPS display, and W/P controls, so their overall approach is consistent. Even among the visible cubes, shading and culling quality differs: attempt 03 appears as a single flat face, attempt 04 has dark edges and a triangle seam, and attempts 01 and 06 show uneven or missing faces. The attempts take the same basic approach but vary a lot in quality. All five are single-file HTML pages with the same palette. All five attempts take a similar dark, single-page landing-page approach, with hero content, program, artists, venue, ticket tiers, FAQ, and inline JavaScript. The six attempts diverge in structure and in how they fail. They share only the broad idea of a canvas game with a 30x30 grid and three mode buttons. I read attempts 1, 3 and 6 in full and compared the screenshots for 1, 2 and 4. I did not open attempts 2, 4 or 5, or shots 3, 5 and 6.

- **Attempt 1:** It declares `const gameOver` as a DOM element and also `function gameOver()`. That redeclaration is a SyntaxError, so the whole script fails to run. Its screenshot shows an empty dark page with only the controls hint, and no menu or canvas. It uses a flat snake array with the head at index 0, a `setInterval` loop and a separate Enter-key state machine. Its CPU code only returns a direction that is never applied.
- **Attempt 2:** Its screenshot shows a different design. A 'Select Mode' menu and a 'Game Over' overlay are drawn on top of each other, with 'Final Score: Player 1: 0 | Player 2: 0'. The layout is overlapping and broken, and it differs from attempt 1.
- **Attempt 3:** The HTML is malformed, with literal text such as `#start-menu` in the body and menu markup that has no container id. It stores the snake with the head at the end of the array. It has a `setInterval` loop, and its CPU logic reacts to the human's keys. The start menu probably cannot work.
- **Attempt 4:** Its screenshot shows only a Score/Mode box and a blank page, with no start menu or canvas visible.
- **Attempt 6:** It uses `Snake` and `Food` classes, `requestAnimationFrame` loops and a 900x900 canvas. It has a high-score entry in `localStorage`, and the game-over handler looks up `#game-over-screen`, which does not exist as an id. The CPU-vs-human loop moves only snake 0.

The approaches differ in snake representation (head first, head last, classes), loop type (`setInterval` or `requestAnimationFrame`), menu architecture and UI layout. Each attempt breaks in a different way, so the output is random rather than consistent.

The attempts diverge in both implementation and visible result. Their code uses different structures, from canvas-based implementations to grid and class-based designs. All six attempts use the same approach: one vanilla HTML/CSS/JS file, a `todos` array saved to localStorage, a `renderTodos` function with a filter, and escapeHtml. Quality varies, though, and attempt 1 is broken.

Attempt 1 calls `escapeHtml()` without defining it, so the first render with a todo throws a ReferenceError. Its `editTodo` also references an undefined `todo`. The footer is a leftover 'Double-click to edit' note that gets overwritten. It is effectively non-functional.

Attempts 2–6 mostly work, with different flaws:
- **Attempt 2:** the toggle uses a delegated click handler on `e.target`, so clicking the SVG or path inside the button does nothing. Its `.stats` element does not exist, so the stats code does nothing.
- **Attempt 3:** the filters sit below the list and work. It has no stats and uses a Delete button.
- **Attempt 4:** it has the most polish, with CSS variables, try/catch storage, a custom key and accessibility attributes. It uses inline `onclick` handlers, and the filter resets to All after toggle, delete or add.

Attempts 2–6 also share a bug: the index in a filtered view is used against the full array, so toggling or deleting in the Active or Completed view hits the wrong item.

The UI, structure, storage keys, toggle mechanism (checkbox, circle, click on text or row), stats presentation and robustness all differ between attempts. Approach is consistent but outcome quality is not, so I rate it 0.5.

The attempts vary substantially in structure and behavior. The six attempts diverge in how they load dat.gui, how they lay out the GUI, and how well they work. I read the code and screenshots 01, 03 and 06. I did not open screenshots 02, 04 or 05.

- **Loading dat.gui:**
  - 01, 02 and 03 use a classic `<script src>` tag, from cdnjs (01, 02) or jsdelivr (03).
  - 04 uses a module `import` of dat.gui.module.js.
  - 05 uses an importmap plus a module import.
  - 06 uses an importmap that points to the minified UMD build, then `import GUI from 'dat.gui'` plus a dynamic script injection.
  - 02 also adds an SRI integrity hash that is likely to fail.
  - These choices differ in how likely they are to work.
- **GUI layout and quality:**
  - Screenshot 01 shows a custom HTML panel with an unlabeled slider panel on the left, and a real dat.gui panel with folders on the right. That is a duplicated GUI.
  - Screenshot 06 shows a custom styled panel with unlabeled sliders and color bars, and no visible dat.gui.
  - Screenshot 03 shows a custom panel with only folder titles and three colored buttons, and no controls.
  - So the GUI ranges from working dat.gui, to a duplicate custom GUI, to a mostly empty or non-functional one.
- **Canvas output:** Every screenshot I opened shows an empty or blank 800x800 canvas area with no visible network, so none of those three showed a clear success. The grep also shows 06 has no `addFolder` or `quadraticCurveTo` matches, unlike 01–05. 06 therefore differs structurally in how it builds the GUI and curves.

The attempts do not share one approach, and their quality varies widely and unpredictably.

All five attempts start from the same skeleton: a single HTML file with a full-window canvas, an 8-vertex cube split into triangles, hand-written rotateX/rotateY, W and P key toggles, and an FPS readout. The shared structure fits a 'consistent approach' reading. Quality and technique vary a lot, though. I did not check the screenshots (shot-01.png is missing). I compared the code only.

- Attempt 1 is the most complete. It does a per-pixel barycentric rasterizer with interpolated Lambert values and a separate wireframe overlay. Its per-vertex normals are wrong (edge vectors), and it culls against the light direction instead of the view direction.
- Attempt 2 uses 4x4 projection matrices and per-pixel scanline fillRect. It culls by light direction, and its resize handler reassigns a const.
- Attempt 3 has no real Gouraud. It builds a path with 10-step edge subdivision and sets fillStyle repeatedly, so the fill ends up a single flat colour. Its rotateY has the wrong sign, and it culls by a rotated normal.
- Attempt 4 is flat-shaded using the average intensity, and it also uses the same face normal for every vertex. It culls by light direction, always draws the white edges, and treats the W key as a no-op for the fill.
- Attempt 5 is the weakest. It has a broken rotateY (z sign), a projection that divides by an unshifted z, a 0.1-alpha clear that leaves trails, and a scanline fill that uses a single colour per row.

The rasterization, lighting, culling and projection techniques therefore differ per attempt, and the output ranges from near-working Gouraud to flat or broken rendering. That is variable quality on a common scaffold, not random divergence of the whole approach.

The attempts diverge in implementation and results. The artifacts do not show comparable quality across attempts.
