Some of the blank screenshots could be capture timing, but as evidence the quality is uneven, with working and apparently non-working outputs from the same approach.

All six attempts use a similar self-contained Canvas 2D cube pipeline, but the results vary sharply: screenshots 01, 02, 05, and 06 show no cube; 03 shows a tiny, dim cube; and 04 shows a clearly visible rotating cube. The shared approach is consistent, but the rendered quality is not.

All six attempts follow the same basic approach. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with a 30x30 grid, a start menu, game-over and restart handling, and a CPU snake driven by a simple heuristic function (getCpuDirection, cpuThink, cpuMove, cpuAI or cpuFindFood). The implementation details vary, though. Attempt 04 renders with a CSS-grid of DOM cells, while the other five use a 600x600 canvas. Attempts 02 and 05 drive the game with requestAnimationFrame, while 01, 03, 04 and 06 use setInterval. Function names and code structure also differ from one attempt to the next. I only compared the code by search and did not run the games or look at the screenshots, so I can't confirm how much their quality actually varies. The differences I did find suggest it varies somewhat, in CPU logic and in game-loop timing.

The attempts vary widely in structure and apparent quality. They use different game architectures, from separate snake variables (01), to a Snake class (03), an array of snakes (04), a frame-based loop (05), and separate human and CPU update paths (06). The screenshots also show inconsistent results: 02 opens on a game-over screen, 04 shows an empty board with no menu, while 01, 03, 05, and 06 show different menu layouts and visual styles. This is substantial divergence across both implementation and presentation.

All six attempts take the same basic approach: a single vanilla HTML/CSS/JS file with a todos array in localStorage, an innerHTML-based render(), and All/Active/Completed filter pills. The UI is similar too, with a card layout and a blue accent. Quality varies a lot, though. Attempt 3 is fully working, with a checkbox, strikethrough, delete, a filter that updates the active pill, and persistence. Attempt 5 is mostly working: it has a circle toggle and escaping, but the filter buttons never update the active class, so the highlighted pill stays on 'All'. Attempt 1 has no UI that can mark a todo complete, since toggleTodo is never wired up. Attempt 2 has the same gap, and the strikethrough can never appear. Attempt 4 wraps everything in an IIFE but uses inline onclick='toggleTodo(...)' and 'deleteTodo(...)', which are not global, so toggle and delete both fail with a ReferenceError. Attempt 6 is the weakest: it compares string dataset ids with numeric ids, so delete and toggle do nothing. It also sets checked="false", which renders the box as checked, has a broken filter-highlight expression, and doesn't escape HTML. Other differences are smaller: new todos are appended in attempts 1 and 3 but prepended in 2, 4 and 5, the checkbox style varies, and the event wiring is either inline or addEventListener. Core features work in only 1 or 2 of the 6 attempts and are broken in different ways in the rest. This is a consistent approach with highly variable quality.

All six use a self-contained HTML todo app with add, filter, completion state, deletion, and localStorage patterns, and attempts 1–5 share a similar centered layout. Quality varies: attempts 1–2 render no way to toggle completion, attempt 4 puts handlers inside an IIFE so its inline toggle/delete calls cannot reach them, and attempt 6 has broken filter highlighting and renders every checkbox as checked. Attempts 3 and 5 implement the core interactions more fully. Attempt 6 also uses a noticeably simpler layout, but the overall approach remains recognizable across attempts.

The attempts diverge widely in structure and in whether they work at all. Attempts 1 and 2 are broken. Attempt 1 throws at GUI setup because it uses `neurons._growTimeout` and the invalid `{ btns.regen }` syntax, and the screenshot shows a blank canvas with no GUI. Attempt 2 hits a ReferenceError on undefined variables such as `threshold`, and its file contains a duplicated document. It shows only a collapsed GUI with an empty canvas and a stray vertical line. Attempt 3 is the only one that renders a working network. It has a full GUI with all folders and buttons, and the canvas shows organic cyan branches, glowing yellow neurons and a synapse. Attempt 4 has a GUI with an extra Neuron Count control but an empty canvas. Attempt 5 renders straight-line cyan and yellow branches with a different control set, and its buttons show up as checkboxes. Attempt 6 has a GUI with different, misplaced color controls and a blank canvas. The structures differ across attempts (class-based, segment-list, per-neuron branch lists, self-calling RAF growth), as do the control labels and the slider ranges and defaults. Quality ranges from fully broken to partly working, and no two attempts look alike, so the results are divergent and effectively random.

Most attempts use the same broad approach: a single canvas, dat.gui controls, and JavaScript for neuron growth, synapses, and pulses. The results vary widely: attempts 1, 4, and 6 show blank canvases; attempt 2 is also nearly blank, with only a tiny, incomplete-looking network; attempt 3 shows a small glowing cluster; and attempt 5 shows a clearer branching network. Attempt 2 additionally contains duplicated full HTML documents. The shared approach is recognizable, but the visible output and implementation consistency are uneven.

The four attempts differ widely in structure and in how well they work. All four use a canvas with greedy Manhattan-distance CPU logic, but they share little else, and their quality is far apart.

Attempt 1 is truncated and broken. The file ends mid-function with stray '</content>' and JSON/markdown garbage, and there is no closing script or HTML. It also has fatal logic errors: it treats the player object as an array (`player1.length`, `unshift`) and the snake state is never a real array. It would not run as a working game. Its start menu is an overlay plus a sidebar <select>, and it uses setInterval.

Attempt 2 is a complete, mostly working game. It uses Snake and Food classes and setInterval. The start menu has mode buttons plus a Start button, and Space/Enter restarts. It has a high score and a localStorage save. Its input handling is odd: it uses keyup/keydown flags, so WASD and the arrow keys control both humans. Its CPU ignores the opponent snake in cvc and hvc.

Attempt 3 is a different design: requestAnimationFrame, with mode buttons that start the game directly. It has serious logic bugs. Human snakes move on every animation frame, so they are far too fast. CPU snakes move twice per tick. Food only respawns on a 2-second timer. The score display shows P1 only. Restart is Enter only, not Space. The canvas is hidden at game over.

Attempt 4 is complete-looking and uses setInterval with a <select> menu and a Space/Enter restart. It has several unusual features: five food items at once, a confirm() dialog on Space, and a Main Menu button. It also contains stray 'n' characters at the start of lines in render() (for example 'n            ctx.fillStyle'). These are syntax errors, so the script fails to parse and the game cannot run.

The screenshots also show four different UI layouts: a sidebar, a mode-button menu with a grid, buttons on a dim canvas, and a select dropdown. Overall quality ranges from non-functional (1 and 4) to playable (2) to buggy (3), with different architectures, so the attempts are divergent.

The attempts vary widely in structure and working state. Attempt 2 uses a Snake class and body arrays; attempt 3 also uses a class but moves human snakes every animation frame while CPU snakes move on a timer, and respawns food on a timer. Attempt 4 switches to object-based snakes and contains stray `n` characters in the render code that make its script invalid. Attempt 1 uses scalar snake coordinates in code that also treats snakes as body arrays, leaving its collision and movement logic inconsistent. The approaches and likely functionality are not consistent across attempts.

All six attempts are broken, and they fail in different ways. None of them draws a cube. Every screenshot is an empty dark canvas with only the HUD, apart from attempt 1, which shows a single thin diagonal line. The code shows the approaches diverging in structure.

Attempt 1 projects raw unscaled coordinates and shades each face with a two-stop linear gradient. Its Lambert term is computed from the vertex position, not a rotated normal. The cube is never rotated, because rotX and rotY stay constant.

Attempt 2 uses a Z-X-Y rotation helper with a hardcoded fake backface-cull vector and a bogus face normal. It fills each triangle with a single flat mid-colour and is capped at 30 fps. Its FPS counter is broken, and it shows 10.

Attempt 3 uses 4x4 matrices, a painter's sort and per-pixel fillRect. It would throw at runtime, because `rotX(rotX)` shadows the function with the variable, and `faces[fi*3+..]` indexes out of range.

Attempt 4 uses a per-pixel putImageData rasteriser. It crashes with a ReferenceError on `fAR`, and it reads `rotX` in its own initialiser, which is a TDZ error. It also colours vertices from a palette string.

Attempt 5 uses per-vertex normals summed over the triangles. It does a scanline fill with fillRect. It reassigns a const (`left`) and uses `r`, `g` and `b` fields that are never defined, so it crashes. Its `M.rotY` also reads `a.cos` on a number.

Attempt 6 uses a fixed 600x600 canvas and 4x4 matrix helpers. It adds an extra R key and builds its triangles per frame. It crashes on an undefined `l`, and its `nx` field is an array.

The approaches differ in rasterisation, normal handling, projection and matrix style. The outcomes differ too, from a stray line to a blank frame, and the FPS readouts range from 60 to 0 to 10. The attempts are not consistent in approach, and the quality is uniformly failed but in unrelated ways, so this is divergent and random.

The attempts share the broad goal of drawing a rotating cube, but use substantially different implementations: direct object-based projection and Canvas gradients in attempt 01, array-based geometry in 02–03, palette-based triangles in 04, and different matrix pipelines in 05–06. Their screenshots are all broken: attempts 02–06 show no cube, while 01 shows only a diagonal line. The approaches diverge and none consistently produces the requested effect.

The attempts share a broad approach but differ wildly in quality, and one is a complete failure. Attempt 03 is degenerate. It stops at line 789 in the middle of a runaway CSS loop of nonsense classes like `.text-yellow-gray-gray-gray…`. It has no closing `</html>`, no body content and no JS. It has no Unsplash images, no SVG map, and no sections, modal, ICS or timeline. Its screenshot (shot-03) is blank black. Attempts 01, 02, 04, 05 and 06 are complete pages of 671 to 1250 lines. All five include `</html>` and the required features. They do vary in polish, though. The hero screenshots differ in headline treatment: 01 puts 'Museum Night, Reimagined' as the headline, while 05 uses 'ARTIFACT: Museum Night' as the main H1. Nav and badge styling differ too. Attempts 02 and 04 show broken hero image alt text ('museum interior') leaking into the layout. Attempt 01 has the fewest lines and the most image/feature-keyword matches. A working-vs-broken split like this, with one unusable output among six, is divergent quality rather than a stable result.

Five attempts (01, 02, and 04–06) use a similar full-length dark event landing-page approach, with hero, program, artist, venue, ticket, FAQ, and calendar features. Their completeness and implementation details vary: attempt 01 has the most image tags and an inline SVG map; 02 has fewer images and no SVG; 04–06 also vary in image and control counts. Attempt 03 is a clear outlier: despite being about the same size, it has no recognizable section, image, button, script, modal, calendar, or FAQ markers. The shared direction across most attempts is consistent, but the outlier and uneven execution make overall stability partial.

All six attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with a 800x800 canvas, dat.gui from a CDN, a branch and synapse model, a requestAnimationFrame loop, and the same section comments. Quality varies a lot. I could only view screenshots for attempts 3 to 6, because shot-01 and shot-02 are missing. Attempt 3 uses a flat GUI with no Growth/Synapses/Pulses/Visuals folders, which the task requires, and its screenshot is blank. Attempt 3 also builds synapses as straight lines between branch tips and is the only one I read in full. Attempt 4 renders a decent glowing network with collapsed folders, but it adds a 'Buttons' folder where the task names four. Attempt 5 has the correct folders and labels, but its screenshot shows only a few short straight stubs. Attempt 6 renders a smeared, oversized magenta blob that looks broken. These are differences in correctness and look, not in architecture, so I rate this 0.5.

The attempts use substantially different simulation structures and produce wildly different results. Attempt 01 grows recursive branches over time; attempt 02 uses Branch and Neuron classes with a different growth model; attempt 03 renders a blank canvas in its screenshot; attempt 04 shows only a few sparse branches; attempt 05 is an intensely overglowing magenta mass; and attempt 06 builds branches immediately through an iterative stack rather than animating growth step by step. Their GUI layouts and control ranges also vary. This is divergent output, not a consistent approach or comparable quality.

All four attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with inline CSS and JS, a dark velvet and gold palette, a Georgia headline, a sticky navbar, and the same hero CTAs. Quality in the hero screenshots varies noticeably, and I did not open the HTML files themselves. Attempt 1 has a left-aligned hero with no image and emoji icons, and the ticket CTA is a bright gold gradient. Attempt 2 has a broken hero: the 'MUSEUM NIGHT, REIMAGINED' badge overlaps the logo and the 'ARTIFACT: Museum Night' headline sits directly under the nav. Its hero is left-aligned with no image, and it never shows the required 'Museum Night, Reimagined' headline in the first view. Attempt 3 has a centered hero and an extra 'Concept' nav link. Its meta block is buggy, with the location split into 'THE OLD GALLERY' and an orphaned ', Warsaw', and a success toast is already visible on load. Attempt 4 has the most polished hero: a centered layout with a visible painterly hero image behind a dark overlay. Its nav has an odd gap between 'Venue' and 'Tickets'. The layout (left-aligned or centered), image use, nav links and visible defects differ between attempts, so quality is inconsistent even though the design direction is shared.

The attempts diverge in both structure and completeness. Attempts 01–03 are long, similarly styled pages with eight sections, but they vary in artist-card count and have substantial implementation issues: attempt 01 contains malformed CSS and has no calendar download; attempt 02 has malformed CSS and also lacks the calendar download; attempt 03 still lacks the calendar download and has no accessible-dialog markup. Attempt 04 is much shorter and takes a different approach, with only six sections, no newsletter, a placeholder venue map, and no artist modal, though it does include a calendar download. None consistently delivers the requested features, and the differing structures and omissions make the attempts unstable.

The attempts diverge in structure and in how they fail, though none of them produces a working cube. I read attempts 01 and 02 in full and compared all six screenshots. I did not read the source of attempts 03–06.

Attempt 01 uses scanline edge intersection with barycentric colour, a fixed 600x600 canvas, and a combined rotation matrix. It applies one flat Lambert colour to all three vertices, so there is no real Gouraud gradient. Its projection and colour scale are broken (`faceColor * dot * 255` with 0–255 colours). Its screenshot shows a single magenta polygon clipped to the canvas edge, at 8 FPS.

Attempt 02 uses a bounding-box barycentric rasterizer, an 800x600 canvas, a 4x4 Float32Array matrix pipeline and a painter's sort. Its lighting is also flat and has a bogus specular term. Its screenshot is an empty dark canvas with FPS 0.

The other screenshots also differ from each other:
- Attempt 03 has an empty black canvas, FPS 0, and an extra arrow-key rotation control in its UI.
- Attempt 04 has a card-style UI with the FPS below the canvas, and shows only a tiny dot at the centre at 61 FPS.
- Attempt 05 has a different styled UI with FPS shown as '--', and an empty canvas.
- Attempt 06 has a light-position readout and no visible canvas or cube at all.

The layout, canvas size, UI, rasterization method, matrix representation and FPS handling all vary between attempts. The visible outcomes also range from a partial polygon to blank canvases to a missing canvas. That is divergent and unreliable, not stable.

All six attempts use the same broad Canvas 2D cube pipeline, but their implementations and visible results vary considerably. The screenshots show no recognizable cube in attempts 2–6: attempt 2 is blank, attempts 3–5 are blank or show only a tiny mark, and attempt 6 shows a tiny fragment. Attempt 1 draws a large magenta polygon spilling off the canvas. The code also diverges in projection, culling, and rasterization details, with apparent issues such as attempt 5 calling `.clear()` on a plain object depth buffer and attempt 6 stopping its render loop when paused. The shared task approach is consistent, but quality is uniformly poor and the failures differ across attempts.

All six attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with a dark neon-green theme, a 30x30 grid, a start menu offering the three modes (Human vs Human, CPU vs Human, CPU vs CPU), arrow keys for one snake and WASD for the other, and a CPU snake. None of the menu screenshots shows a broken attempt. The quality and details vary between attempts, though. I judged this from the six screenshots and a keyword-count grep; I did not read the code in full or play the games. Differences I saw:
- Starting a game: attempt 1 starts as soon as you press 1, 2 or 3. Attempts 2, 3 and 4 select a mode with 1/2/3 and then need Enter. Attempt 5 adds a Start button that also accepts Space. Attempt 6 shows plain mode buttons with no number hints.
- Layout and look: attempts 1, 2 and 5 are monospace with a glowing frame. Attempt 3 has a card-style menu and attempt 6 a sans-serif menu inside the canvas. Attempt 2 shows two score labels at the top of the menu screen and attempt 6 shows one. Attempts 1, 3, 4 and 5 show no score on the menu screen.
- Controls: in CPU vs Human, attempts 2 and 3 let the human use either arrow keys or WASD, while attempts 5 and 6 allow arrows only. Attempt 6 adds an M key to return to the menu.
- Colours: attempt 3 uses green and orange for the two snakes, and attempt 2 uses green and red.

The core approach is consistent, but the UX and control details vary, so this is 0.5 rather than 1.

All six use a browser-based canvas game with a menu and three mode choices, so the overall approach is recognizable across attempts. Quality and details vary: attempts 1–4 and 6 show mode-specific menus, while attempt 5’s screenshot shows only a single-player menu and score; the menu layouts and controls also differ, and attempt 1 uses keyboard-only mode selection while others show clickable buttons. The screenshots show menus rather than gameplay, so they do not establish consistent in-game behavior.

All 6 attempts are the same kind of app: one HTML file with vanilla JS, a `todos` array of {id,text,completed}, a render() that rebuilds the list, and a localStorage key. All six also include the four core features, filters, an items-left counter and a 'Clear completed' button, and I see no functional bugs in any of them. Every attempt would pass the stated requirements, so the core is stable. Quality and design vary in ways that matter. (1) Look: 1 has a purple header band, 2 a white card on a purple gradient, 3 a blue gradient, 4 a pink/blue gradient, 5 a purple gradient with a circular custom checkbox, and 6 a pale background with gradient-text heading. (2) Interaction: 1 and 3 animate removal; the others delete instantly. 1 has a custom SVG checkbox with a label; 2, 3, 4 and 6 use native checkboxes; 5 uses a div checkbox that is not keyboard-accessible. Attempts 5 and 6 have no aria-labels on the checkboxes (5 has no semantic checkbox at all); 1, 2 and 3 are fuller on accessibility. (3) Form handling: 1, 2, 3 and 5 use a form submit; 4 and 6 use a click handler plus a keydown Enter handler. (4) Robustness: 1, 3 and 6 validate loaded data, 2 only checks that it is an array, 4 doesn't validate at all, and 4 and 5 only partly do so. 2 and 5 don't guard `setItem` against errors. (5) Clear-completed behaviour: attempts 1, 2, 3 and 5 hide or disable it when nothing is completed; 4 and 6 always show it. (6) Code style: attempt 5 uses `var` and event delegation, while the others use `const` and per-element listeners. This is consistent core quality with noticeable polish and robustness differences, not a divergence in approach, so 0.5.

All six attempts use the same basic single-page todo structure and implement adding, completion toggles, deletion, filters, and localStorage. Their quality varies: attempts 01–03 and 05 use different layouts and storage keys; attempt 05 uses a clickable div for completion instead of a checkbox, while attempt 06 toggles completion by clicking the text as well as the checkbox. The screenshots also show noticeably different card layouts, spacing, and color schemes. The approach is consistent, but the details and interaction quality are uneven.

The attempts diverge in architecture and in whether they work at all. The screenshots show wildly different results. Attempt 1 draws a few short straight line stubs with magenta neuron dots. Attempt 2 shows only four yellow-green dots and no branches. Attempt 3 shows a completely empty canvas. Attempt 4 is the best: a branching network with a glow, synapse dots and an HUD, plus Show Grid and Show Scanlines toggles. Attempt 6 also shows an empty canvas. Attempt 5 has no screenshot. Its code uses setInterval for growth and pulses, with an updating `Branch` class that only renders branches once they have finished, and `regenerate` wired to every slider's onChange. It also has duplicate config keys, and its Visuals and Controls folders are named differently from the others. The GUI layouts and folder naming also differ: the Actions, Buttons and Controls folders, and a collapsed versus open panel. Quality ranges from working to blank, and the implementations are structured differently, so the attempts are not stable.

The attempts vary widely in visible result: attempt 01 shows only a few short branches, attempt 02 shows seed dots without branches, attempt 03 is blank with its controls collapsed, attempt 04 shows a developed branching network, and attempt 06 is blank. Although the files share a canvas, dat.gui, and animation loop, their output quality is inconsistent rather than comparable across attempts.

The attempts share one approach but differ in quality. All six are single-file HTML with the same function-based layout: the same four dat.gui folders, a tip-based growth step, quadraticCurveTo branches, synapse detection, pulses, a vignette and a requestAnimationFrame loop. Their visible output varies a lot, judging from the screenshots and from grep-ing the source (I did not run the files).

Attempt 5 is broken. Its screenshot shows only the empty background glow, with no GUI panel and no network. Its dat.gui script URL uses a different path (`dat.gui/0.7.9`) from the others (`dat-gui/0.7.9`), which likely fails to load.

Attempt 4 inlines dat.gui, unlike the other five, which load it from a CDN. Its screenshot has a muddy yellow vignette that tints the whole canvas, which breaks the intended dark look.

Attempt 2 grows a dense tree with many synapse dots, while attempts 1, 3 and 6 show only a few sparse branches. Attempt 1 has plain cyan lines with no accent color or synapses. Attempt 3 shows green-tinted branches. Attempt 6 is neat but has few synapses.

The approach is consistent, but one attempt is outright broken, one has a visible rendering flaw, and the rest differ in density and glow, so I rate this 0.5.

All six attempts follow the same basic approach: a single canvas animation with dat.gui folders, neon branches, and controls for growth, synapses, pulses, and visuals. Their results vary substantially, though: attempts 01, 02, and 04 show developed networks, while 03 and 06 show sparse, disconnected branches, and 05 renders no network at all. Attempt 04 also has a much stronger yellow background glow than the others. The shared structure is consistent, but the visible quality is not.

All four attempts take the same basic approach: one vanilla HTML/CSS/JS file with a todos array of {id: Date.now(), text, completed}, a render function, escapeHtml, a localStorage save/load, and All/Active/Completed filters. All four cover the five requirements. Quality and style still vary. Attempt 2 has a CSS typo (`border: 2px solid #e0e0e0;\            background: white;`) that drops the filter button background declaration. It also adds try/catch around storage, which the others lack. Attempt 3 uses a flat grey/blue look with no gradient, per-element addEventListener, an init() function and a scrollable list. The other three share a purple gradient card look. Attempt 4 uses inline onclick handlers and an emoji title. Its setFilter relies on the implicit global `event`, which is fragile. It also adds per-filter empty messages and a gradient button style. New todos are appended in attempts 1 and 3 but prepended in attempts 2 and 4. Delete buttons are always visible in attempts 1 and 4 but hover-only in attempts 2 and 3. The empty state, stats text and event-wiring style also differ. The approach is consistent but polish, robustness and UI details are not.

All four attempts use the same basic single-page todo approach and include adding, completing, deleting, filtering, and localStorage persistence. Quality is uneven: attempt 2 has a malformed CSS declaration, attempt 4 shows corrupted text in its heading and relies on the global event object for filter clicks, while attempts 1 and 3 avoid those visible issues. The layouts and styling also vary noticeably, though the core structure remains consistent.

All six attempts use the same approach. Each is a software rasterizer that writes to an ImageData buffer and calls putImageData on a Canvas 2D context. Each has a rotating cube, backface culling, per-vertex Lambert lighting, W and P key handlers and an FPS counter. The differences are in structure and rendering quality. Attempts 03 and 04 use a z-buffer. Attempts 02, 05 and 06 use a painter's-algorithm depth sort, and attempt 01 does neither. The screenshots also differ. Attempt 02 is a small, vividly coloured cube with a visible seam artifact. Attempt 03 is cropped to a single flat yellow face, which looks like a camera or scale problem. Attempts 01 and 06 are very large and dark, and attempt 01's cube is clipped by the canvas edges and has a barely visible dark shading. Attempts 04 and 05 are well framed with good colours. HUD layout and canvas sizing also vary. The approach is consistent, but the framing, scale, lighting brightness and depth handling vary from attempt to attempt.

The attempts use noticeably different implementations and produce widely different results. Attempt 01 shows an oversized, clipped cube; attempt 02 shows a much smaller cube with visible triangle seams; attempt 03 produces a clear, well-framed cube; attempt 04 is oversized and clipped; attempt 05 is clear and well-framed; and attempt 06 is again oversized and clipped. Their rasterization, depth handling, sizing, and HUD layouts also vary, so the quality is not consistent across attempts.

All six attempts take the same approach: one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and JS, a Georgia serif headline over a dark burgundy-to-near-black spotlight hero, and gold gradient CTAs and pills. All six appear to implement the ICS download, the modals with Escape handling, and scroll-reveal via IntersectionObserver. Grep counts of those feature markers are similar across files (6–11 each). Quality and design vary between them. The hero layout differs: 01, 03, 04, 05 and 06 are centered; 02 is left-aligned; 03 is left-aligned with a bold gold headline and a plain-text date line instead of badges. Badge and button styling also differs: 05 and 06 use emoji icons and rounded pill buttons, while 01 to 04 use square buttons or pills with no emoji, and 01 has an extra intro paragraph. In every screenshot the hero image does not render and the hero shows only a gradient, so the shared flaw is the same. I only reviewed the hero screenshots and grep counts, not the full pages, so deeper sections such as the venue map, timeline and checkout were not compared. With a consistent approach and noticeable variation in design and polish, this lands at 0.5.

All six attempts use a similar single-file structure and share the same dark, gold-accented ARTIFACT landing-page concept, with sections and code for tickets, FAQs, newsletter signup, and calendar downloads. The screenshots also show a broadly consistent centered hero and sticky navigation, but the visual execution varies: attempt 01 adds more hero copy, while 02–06 use different layouts and spacing, and none visibly shows the requested museum imagery. Implementation coverage also varies: attempts 01, 02, 04, and 05 include nine or ten image elements, while 03 and 06 have only two; attempt 03 also lacks the exact headline phrase. This is a consistent approach with noticeable quality and completeness differences, rather than equally stable results or wholly divergent approaches.

All six attempts take the same approach. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with an overlay start menu offering the three modes (human vs human, CPU vs human, CPU vs CPU). Each has a two-snake arena: snake 1 on the arrow keys and snake 2 on WASD. Each shows a live two-score HUD, a game-over overlay with a restart keypress (R, Enter or Space), a fixed `setInterval` tick, and a greedy distance-to-food CPU with collision avoidance (no full BFS pathfinding). Most use a neon dark theme, and four of them (2, 4, 5, 6) share the title 'Neon Snake Arena' or 'Neon Serpents'. The differences are small. Attempt 1 renders the grid as 900 DOM divs with a radio-button menu and a 'Dual Snake Arena' title, while attempts 2–6 draw on a canvas. Attempt 2 adds a d-pad and a CPU that frees its own tail cell and breaks distance ties by open space, while attempt 1's CPU is the simplest. Attempt 1 reads only attempt 1 and 2 in full; for 3–6 I confirmed only the canvas, `setInterval`, and a CPU direction function by grep, so their quality is inferred rather than verified. Of the two I read in full, none appears broken or missing a required feature, and quality looks comparable.

All six attempts build a two-snake arena with a 30×30 board, scores, start and game-over screens, keyboard controls, and the three requested modes. Attempts 02–06 use a canvas-based board with broadly similar gameplay, while attempt 01 takes a distinct DOM-grid approach and uses a different menu and layout. The core approach is mostly consistent, but that structural difference makes the set less than fully stable.

All six attempts use the same approach and reach comparable quality. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with vanilla JS wrapped in an IIFE and no framework. Each keeps a `todos` array of `{id, text, completed}` in localStorage, validated and wrapped in try/catch on load. Each re-renders the whole list from `render()` with DOM-built `<li>` items and a checkbox, a label or span, and a delete button. Each implements the same four requirements: add (trim, ignore empty, unshift), complete (strikethrough via `text-decoration: line-through`), delete, and All/Active/Completed filters using `aria-pressed`. All six also have an empty state, an items-left counter, and responsive CSS with a purple gradient card. I found no functional bugs in any of them. The differences are cosmetic or minor extras. Attempts 1 and 6 add a 'Clear completed' button, and attempt 6 also persists the selected filter. Delete is an SVG icon in most attempts but a text 'Delete' button in attempts 3 and 6. Attempts 4 and 5 use a round custom checkbox. Layout, titles and the localStorage key name also vary. Attempt 2's `saveTodos` has no try/catch, a minor robustness gap. These are stylistic and feature-polish variations on the same design, not differences in approach or in whether the app works.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a self-contained vanilla HTML/CSS/JS todo app with localStorage, an add form, completion checkboxes with strikethrough styling, delete controls, and All/Active/Completed filters. The screenshots show polished purple-accented task-list interfaces throughout. Layouts and labels vary, but the attempts reach comparable quality without any visibly broken outlier.

All six attempts follow the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with 8 sections, a serif headline, and a gold-on-near-black palette. Quality and execution vary noticeably, based on the screenshots and a count of Unsplash URLs in each file. Hero layout: attempt 1 has a plain left-aligned dark hero with no visible image, a stat box, and a doubled 'Get Tickets' button in the navbar whose text is illegible. Attempts 2 and 4 use a full-bleed museum photo. Attempt 3 uses a split layout with a framed photo on the right. Attempts 5 and 6 are image-less gradient or black heroes with centered or offset text. Image handling: attempts 1 and 5 have 18 Unsplash URLs each and attempt 6 has 9. Attempts 2, 3 and 4 have none in the HTML source, so they presumably load images another way. Attempt 5 also shows stray alt text leaking under the navbar, which suggests a broken image. Attempt 1 has the visible navbar bug. Hero polish and cinematic feel range from strong (2, 3, 4) to bare (1, 6). The approach is consistent, but visible quality and layout choices differ between attempts.

All six attempts follow the same dark, gold-accented ARTIFACT landing-page approach and include the main event sections, ticket tiers, artist cards, and interaction patterns. Quality varies visibly: attempts 3–4 show a strong museum image and polished split or full-bleed hero, while attempt 1’s hero is mostly empty and attempts 5–6 have little or no visible hero imagery (attempt 5 also shows broken-image alt text). The layouts and program details also vary, so the results are consistent in approach but uneven in execution.

All six attempts use the same basic design: a single 800x800 canvas, dat.gui from a CDN, quadratic-curve branches, the neon palette, and shadowBlur glow. Each has the four folders, the three buttons and a vignette, and each has a setup, GUI, growth, synapse, pulse and render layout. Synapses are straight lines between branch tips, and pulses are dots that move along those lines. Quality and behavior differ a lot between attempts, though. (1) Attempt 1 is sparse. Growth stalls after a few branches, and synapses are rebuilt in full on every branch finish. It has a dat.gui-missing fallback and a text overlay. (2) Attempt 2 produces a dense mesh of about 1129 synapse links, which swamps the branches in magenta. Its neuron count is also off, because the screenshot shows three bright dots in the middle. (3) Attempt 3 is compact and balanced. It adds a fallback synapse so at least one link always exists, and its branch sprouting is more varied. (4) Attempt 4 shows large magenta blobs, with a clear synapse and pulse look. It has a different growth mechanism, using a random-delay child-spawn timer, and a larger default depth. (5) Attempt 5 randomizes neuron count at load. Its growth is one long chain per neuron, it has few synapses at the moment of the screenshot, and the GUI shows raw property names. Its pause button also relabels itself. (6) Attempt 6 grows a few segments per frame from a queue rather than animating along each branch. Its screenshot shows a yellow-tinted overlay on the canvas and blank folder titles in the GUI. The visible spread is wide, from sparse (1, 5) to over-dense (2, 4) to a small cluster (3) to a broken GUI style (6). There are also real functional differences: some attempts have an on-canvas HUD, some call regenerate on slider change and some don't, and the GUI labels vary. That gives a consistent approach with variable quality and look.

All six attempts follow the same general approach: a single canvas with animated branching growth, dat.gui folders, synapses, pulses, and neon colors. Quality varies substantially: attempt 02 shows a dense, polished network with all controls visible, while attempt 05 shows sparse, disconnected branches and collapsed control folders; attempt 01 is still growing with only a small cluster, and attempt 03 has unusually strong synapse glow settings. Attempts 04 and 06 also use the same overall design but differ in growth and visual results. The approach is consistent, but the rendered quality and completeness vary.

The six attempts share a broad idea (a CPU rasterizer with putImageData, barycentric interpolation, a Lambert-lit cube) but diverge in design and in how well they work. Quality varies widely, from a visible cube to a blank screen to a white bug.

Structure and approach:
- Attempt 1 uses a monochrome teal material and painter's-sorted triangles with no depth buffer. Its normals are averaged per vertex and it has an HTML HUD with buttons.
- Attempt 2 uses per-face colours, a depth buffer with 1/z, and a compact HUD. FPS and state sit in one text line.
- Attempt 3 uses a depth buffer, a matrix-based pipeline, per-vertex normals taken from the vertex position, and a perspective grid floor.
- Attempt 4 uses painter's sorting and reads the frame with getImageData. Its canvas-size handling is different.
- Attempt 5 draws the HUD on the canvas itself and has no HTML HUD.
- Attempt 6 uses per-face colours, per-triangle normals and a partial-region ImageData. Its HUD is a two-panel layout.

Outcomes in the screenshots:
- Attempt 1 shows a plausible shaded teal cube, but the whole thing looks flat and nearly monochrome.
- Attempt 2 shows a nearly invisible, very dark green square.
- Attempt 3 shows the best result: a clearly shaded cube with a grid floor.
- Attempt 4 shows a dim, dark cube.
- Attempt 5 shows no cube at all, only the background and the HUD. Its backface-cull axis mapping is likely broken.
- Attempt 6 shows a visible rendering bug: a white rectangular block around the cube. The ImageData is initialised transparent and the putImageData call overwrites the background with it.

One attempt is blank, one has a glaring artifact, and the rest range from dark to well lit. The approaches, the colour schemes (monochrome, per-face and blue), the depth handling and the HUD design all differ, so this is divergent output with random quality.

All six attempts use a Canvas 2D cube renderer with triangle rasterization and lighting, but quality varies sharply. Attempt 01 shows a large, bright cube and a detailed HUD; attempts 02–04 show very dark, nearly featureless cube faces; attempt 05 shows no cube in its screenshot; and attempt 06 has a conspicuous black rectangle behind the cube. The artifacts share a broad approach, but their visible results are inconsistent.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with a canvas-rendered 30x30 grid, a dark-themed overlay UI, and a TICK_MS constant of 115 in the four attempts whose code I checked (01, 02, 03, 04). Each has a menu overlay, a pause overlay, a game-over overlay, a two-snake model with human and CPU controllers, and a BFS food-seeker with a flood-fill fallback. I read attempts 01 and 04 in full and only grepped 02, 03, 05 and 06, so the similarity of those four is inferred from the grep matches. Quality also looks broadly comparable, since none of the six looks broken.

The differences are in implementation details and UX choices, not in whether the game works:
- **Menu flow:** attempt 01 starts immediately when a mode button is clicked, or when 1/2/3 is pressed. Attempt 04 has a select-a-mode step followed by a separate Start button. Attempts 02, 03 and 05 also use aria-pressed mode selection.
- **Control mapping:** attempt 01 gives arrows to Player 1 and WASD to Player 2. Attempt 04 reverses this, with WASD for Player 1 and arrows for Player 2. In CPU vs Human, the human snake therefore ends up on different keys across attempts.
- **Restart key:** attempt 01 restarts on Enter, and attempt 04 on R or Enter. Attempt 03 has R and Enter handlers, and attempt 02 has an R handler.
- **Implementation details:** the loop is a setInterval in 01, a requestAnimationFrame accumulator in 04, and setInterval plus requestAnimationFrame in 05. Cell size is 30 in attempts 01 and 05 and 20 in 02, 03 and 04.
- **Scoring:** attempt 01 scores 1 per food, and attempt 04 scores 10 per food plus a separate food counter.
- **Visual theme:** the palettes and layouts differ (green and blue in 01, cyan and pink neon in 04).

These are variations on one design with similar overall quality, so the attempts are consistent in approach but vary in detail. I rate this 0.5 rather than 1 because the control mappings, menu flow and restart keys differ in ways a player would notice.

All six attempts follow the same overall approach: a single-file canvas Snake game with a 30×30 board, three selectable human/CPU modes, scores, and menu/game-over UI. Their presentation varies, from the large centered arcade menus in attempts 01 and 04 to the sidebar layouts in 02, 05, and 06 and the neon duel layout in 03. The implementations also differ in control and game flow: for example, attempt 02 has a separate Start game step after choosing a mode, while several others start directly from the mode choice; key bindings and CPU pathfinding strategies vary. The screenshots show polished, comparably complete menus across the set, with no obvious outlier, but the designs and details are not identical enough to call them fully stable.

All six attempts use the same approach and reach comparable quality. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with vanilla JS wrapped in an IIFE and a todos array of {id, text, completed}. Each saves to localStorage with try/catch, parses defensively on load, and re-renders by rebuilding the list with replaceChildren. Each has a checkbox that toggles a line-through style, a delete button, and All/Active/Completed filters via aria-pressed buttons. Each has an items-left count, an empty state, a hidden label, and a responsive media query, and each covers every required feature with no broken attempt. The differences are cosmetic or minor. Attempts 1, 4 and 6 use an indigo palette and attempts 2, 3 and 5 a green/sage one. Some use a serif heading. The filters sit in the toolbar or the footer. Delete is an SVG or an '×'. New todos use push (1, 2, 3, 4) or unshift (5, 6). Some announce changes through aria-live regions. Attempt 5 hides the delete button until hover on desktop, and attempt 6 doesn't reset the filter to All after adding. These are small variations in polish, not differences in approach or in whether the app works.

All six attempts use the same self-contained HTML/CSS/JavaScript pattern: an add form, checkbox-based completion with strikethrough, delete controls, All/Active/Completed filters, and localStorage persistence. They all appear to implement the requested behavior with comparable quality. Styling, labels, empty states, and storage key names vary, but there is no major structural or functional divergence.

All six attempts take the same approach and look like the same design. Each is a single self-contained HTML file of similar size, with 18–20 source.unsplash references. Each has the same dark velvet and gold look: a sticky navbar with a gold 'Get Tickets' button, and a hero with a huge serif 'Museum Night,' over an italic soft-gold 'Reimagined'. Below that comes the 'ARTIFACT: Museum Night' line, the date/time/place row, and gold 'Get Tickets' and outlined 'Save to Calendar' buttons. The screenshots differ only in small ways. Attempts 2–5 show the same hero painting, while attempts 1 and 6 show a dark spotlight with no image, most likely because the remote image had not loaded when the screenshot was taken. The eyebrow text, the placement of the vertical side text, the logo mark (diamond, triangle or boxed A) and the CTA wording ('Reserve your place' in attempt 1) also vary. Attempts 1, 2, 4 and 6 each have 8 'View details' strings. Attempts 3 and 5 have none, so they most likely use a different label for the artist-card button, but both still have an artist modal with a bio. I did not open the files to compare the timeline, venue, ticket or FAQ sections, the .ics code or the other interactions. These are only surface differences, so the attempts are comparable in approach and quality.

All six attempts use the same dark, gold-accented editorial landing-page approach, with a sticky navigation bar, oversized serif hero, and the requested event sections. Quality and completeness vary: screenshots 01 and 06 show a mostly blank hero, while 02–05 show a large painting; attempts 03 and 04 lack the specified calendar start time in their markup, and the ticket flow, active navigation, and interaction details differ across files. The overall approach is consistent, but not the implementation quality.

All six attempts use the same approach and reach about the same quality. Each is a single HTML file that renders a software rasterizer into an ImageData buffer on Canvas 2D. Each defines 8 vertices and 6 quad faces split into 2 triangles, and rotates with sin/cos matrices. Each uses perspective projection with a fixed camera distance and culls backfaces with a dot-product test. Each computes per-vertex Lambert lighting from a point light that orbits the cube, and interpolates the vertex RGB with barycentric weights. All of them implement W (wireframe) and P (pause) as both keys and buttons, show an FPS readout from a roughly 0.5 s sampling window, and wrap the canvas in a dark HUD with similar styling. All of them appear functionally complete.

The differences are minor implementation details, not differences in whether it works:
- Depth handling: attempts 2, 3, 4 and 5 use a per-pixel z-buffer, while 1 and 6 use painter's sorting.
- Lighting normals: attempts 3 and 6 use averaged vertex normals, so shading is smoother across edges. The others use flat face normals.
- Wireframe: attempts 1 and 2 draw it as a mode or overlay, and 6 draws only the cube edges.
- Extras: attempt 4 adds a Restart button and R key, and attempt 6 puts the canvas inside a card layout instead of fullscreen.
- Rendering resolution: attempts 1 and 2 render at reduced resolution and scale up.

These cause small visual and structural variation, but no attempt is broken or markedly weaker than the rest.

All six attempts use the same broad approach: a self-contained Canvas 2D cube demo with rotation, perspective projection, lighting, FPS, and wireframe/pause controls. Their rendered results vary sharply, though: screenshots 01, 02, 03, and 05 show essentially a single flat face; 04 shows three dim faces and a light marker; 06 shows a more recognizable two-face cube. The shared structure is consistent, but the visual quality and apparent correctness are not.

All six attempts take the same approach. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with a canvas-based 30x30 neon-themed two-snake arena. Each uses a setInterval tick loop (attempt 04 uses requestAnimationFrame with a timestamp). Each has a start menu offering the three modes (Human vs Human, CPU vs Human, CPU vs CPU) and 1/2/3 and Enter/Space controls. P1 uses WASD and P2 uses arrow keys. Each has a live score HUD for two players, pause and restart handling, and a game-over screen. The CPU is a BFS/flood-fill pathfinder with open-space safety checks in every attempt: distanceToFood/openSpace in 01, explore/frontDistance in 02, floodSearch in 04 and floodArea in 05. Function structure is also very similar across them: spawnFood or placeFood, startGame, showMenu, finish, chooseCpuDirection, tick, draw. The screenshots show the same dark neon look and the same menu pattern, differing only in layout, wording and accent colours. Attempt 02 adds a sidebar and attempt 04 uses a mode-card row. These are cosmetic differences, and I found no broken or clearly weaker attempt. I judged this from the screenshots and function structure and did not run the games, so quality parity rests on that evidence.

All six attempts use a polished dark arcade presentation and implement the same two-snake game with the three requested modes and CPU control. Their overall approach is consistent, but the layouts and interaction designs vary substantially: attempt 2 uses a wide arena with a separate match-status and controls sidebar, attempts 3–5 use selectable mode cards with a separate start action, while attempts 1 and 6 put mode buttons directly in a centered overlay. The score displays, branding, and menu navigation also differ, so the results are not comparably consistent in presentation and interaction.

All six attempts are a single-file vanilla HTML/CSS/JS todo app with the same structure and about the same quality. Each has a text input and an 'Add task' submit button, a checkbox that toggles completion, and a delete button per item. Each has All/Active/Completed filter buttons using aria-pressed, a 'N tasks left/remaining' counter, and a filter-specific empty state. Each uses a render() function that rebuilds the list, an IIFE or module-level script, textContent (no innerHTML injection), and localStorage with try/catch around load and save plus validation of loaded entries. Strikethrough comes from a .completed class (or a :checked sibling selector in attempt 3). All six look functionally correct on a read-through; I did not run them or open the screenshots.

The differences are mostly cosmetic or minor. The visual theme varies: warm beige (1, 2), green (3), teal with a stats dashboard (4), a navy hero with indigo accents (5), and a plain indigo card (6). Layout details differ: attempt 4 adds stat tiles and filter counts, and attempt 5 adds a hero banner. New todos go to the end in attempts 1, 2, 5 and 6 (push) and to the top in attempts 3 and 4 (unshift). Delete is a ×, an SVG icon or the word 'Delete', and attempt 3 renders the empty state as an li. Attempt 5 validates stored items less strictly (no id uniqueness check), and attempt 6 repairs missing ids rather than dropping the item. None of these changes whether the requirements are met, so the approach and quality are consistent.

The attempts take noticeably different approaches and produce distinct designs: attempts 1–3 use different editorial card layouts, attempt 4 is a dashboard with summary counts, attempt 5 has a full-width hero above the app, and attempt 6 uses a compact purple card. The implementation details also vary, including different storage keys, markup, and interaction patterns. They generally include adding, completing, deleting, filtering, and localStorage persistence, so quality is broadly comparable, but the approaches diverge enough across all six to indicate instability.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with an 800×800 canvas, dat.gui folders for Growth, Synapses, Pulses and Visuals, and the neon palette. Each has cyan main branches, yellow-green accent branches, magenta synapses and yellow pulses, a grid, a vignette, and a framed page header and footer. The screenshots show that quality and look vary noticeably, though. Attempt 1 is a dense magenta blob at the centre with sparse branches. Attempts 2 and 3 look good, but attempt 2 has long straight branches and wide purple link lines, and attempt 3 is a dense, tangled mesh. Attempt 4 has a large heading and a telemetry block and shows neuron nodes, but its canvas is pushed below the fold. Attempt 5 is small and compact with visible nodes. Attempt 6 uses a restyled yellow GUI, with the regenerate button placed in the Growth folder. Page layout, GUI styling (including button placement), branch density and growth parameters (split chance ranges from 0.075 to 0.72) differ between attempts. Overall quality is comparable, but the visual results and polish are inconsistent. I did not read the HTML source because the shell command was blocked, so this judgement rests on the screenshots alone.

All six attempts use the same core approach: a single canvas with a dat.gui panel, animated branching neurons, synapses, and pulses, in a similar neon-on-dark style. Their visual results vary noticeably, though: attempt 01 has a tight, crowded magenta center with sparse outer branches; attempts 02 and 03 show much denser networks; attempt 05 is comparatively sparse; and attempts 04 and 06 use different layouts and framing. The structure is consistent, but the apparent density and polish are not comparable across attempts.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with an 800×800 canvas, dat.gui, the same neon palette, and the Growth/Synapses/Pulses/Visuals folders. Each has the three buttons, quadratic-curve branches, shadowBlur glow, a vignette and scanlines. Grep counts of addFolder, quadraticCurveTo and createRadialGradient are similar across files (8–9 each). The output differs a lot in look and behavior, though. The screenshots were taken at different growth stages, so some of the difference may be timing. Attempt 1 has a dense, wide web of magenta synapses, with a title and a status label. Attempt 2 has only a few long sparse branches, a single tiny synapse cluster, and a Visuals folder open. Attempt 3 has a tree-like dendrite with no visible synapses at all. Attempt 4 shows only four tiny spark dashes at the start of growth, with a visible horizontal grid and no network yet. Attempt 5 has thick smooth curves, a few synapse nodes and yellow tip dots. Attempt 6 has jittery, noisy branches, very dense synapses, and a yellow-themed GUI. Growth-speed ranges (1.3, 1.4, 2.4, 12, 62), branch styles, HUD text and GUI styling also vary. This is a consistent structure with noticeably variable visual quality and completeness, so it scores 0.5.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a single neon canvas, dat.gui folders, branching growth, synapse links, and animated pulses. Their results vary substantially, though: the screenshots range from sparse, nearly unbranched networks in attempts 04 and 05 to a dense web of synapses in 06, with 01–03 falling between those extremes. The controls and visual styling remain broadly consistent, but the network density and overall result are not comparable across attempts.

The six attempts take essentially the same approach. Each is a single HTML file of roughly 61–72 KB, with a dark gold-and-burgundy cinematic theme and a sticky nav with a gold 'Get Tickets' CTA. The hero uses a Georgia serif headline 'Museum Night, Reimagined' with an italic gold second line, a left-aligned text block, a dark overlay with gradient, and 'Get Tickets' and 'Save to Calendar' buttons. All six have a date/time/place strip and a vertical side caption, and all include the .ics generator, inline SVG and Unsplash URLs. Quality varies visibly in the screenshots. Attempt 5 has a layout bug: the hero text and the metadata row sit flush against the left viewport edge with no padding. Attempt 2 omits the 'ARTIFACT: Museum Night' subtitle line that the other attempts show, and it has a washed-out, bright hero image. Attempt 1 is the most polished, with a cohesive dark floral hero and badge-like metadata. Attempts 3, 4 and 6 are polished and similar to each other. Match counts for the key features also vary by file (attempt 3 has 3 matches against 11–14 in attempts 2, 4, 5 and 6), which suggests different implementation depth. The hero images differ between attempts because the Unsplash random endpoint returns a different photo each time, so they vary in mood and legibility. Overall this is a consistent approach with variable polish and some defects.

All six attempts take the same polished, single-file landing-page approach: a dark, gold-accented cinematic hero with oversized serif type, event details, ticket and calendar buttons, followed by the same museum-event sections and interactive features. Their sizes are comparable (about 61–72 KB), and each includes the calendar download, a map, and a ticket or artist modal. The screenshots show comparable visual quality and layout. The main variation is the hero imagery—some choices are less relevant to a museum night, such as a wine glass or abstract liquid—but that does not make the overall approaches or quality diverge.

All six attempts use the same core approach: a software Gouraud rasterizer that writes into an ImageData buffer on Canvas 2D (no WebGL). Each has W and P toggles, an FPS readout, and a dark-themed page with UI chrome around the cube. The visual quality and framing vary noticeably. I judged this from the screenshots and from a grep of the code for the ImageData calls, without reading each file in full. Attempts 1–4 show the cube so close that one face fills the view, so it barely reads as a cube. Attempts 5 and 6 show a full cube with several faces visible and look correct. Lighting also differs. Attempt 3's visible face is almost unlit, a flat dark purple with no visible gradient. Attempt 5's faces are dark and nearly flat. Attempts 1, 2, 4 and 6 show clear Gouraud gradients. Attempt 4 has a layout bug: the canvas panel overlaps the text panel and clips the headline and stats. The layout and page design also differ in every attempt: sidebar stats, a hero heading, a panel layout, and so on. So the approach is consistent, but the final quality and visual result are variable.

All six use a similar self-contained Canvas 2D pipeline with cube geometry, triangle rasterization, lighting, animation, and W/P controls. But the results vary substantially: screenshots 01–04 show a single flat quadrilateral with little or no visible per-vertex shading, while 05–06 show a recognizable rotating cube with multiple visible faces and stronger lighting variation. The shared approach is consistent, but the rendered quality is not.

All 6 attempts take the same approach and meet every requirement. Each is a single vanilla-JS HTML file with an in-memory todos array and a render() that rebuilds the list. Each has an add form with trim and empty-check, a checkbox toggle with line-through on completed items, delete, All/Active/Completed filter buttons, an 'N items left' counter, an empty state, and try/catch-guarded localStorage save and load. I read the code and found no functional bug in any of them. The differences are cosmetic or minor extras. Attempts 3 and 4 add a 'Clear completed' button. Attempts 3, 4 and 6 persist the filter. Attempt 5 uses a purple gradient background and a text 'Delete' button, and attempt 5 also persists with a bare 'todos' key and has no load validation. Attempt 2 builds rows with innerHTML plus an escape function while the others use createElement. Attempt 6 uses const/let and a state object where the rest use var. The storage keys and visual themes also vary. None of this changes the core behaviour or the overall quality.

All six use the same basic approach: a single-page todo app with an input, All/Active/Completed filters, a rendered list with completion and delete controls, and localStorage persistence. The layouts and styling vary—some use a gradient background or header, while others use a plain card, and attempts 3 and 4 add a clear-completed control—but the core structure and apparent quality remain comparable across attempts.

All six attempts take the same approach and reach about the same quality. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with a 600x600 canvas (30x30 grid, 20px cells) and a requestAnimationFrame or tick loop. All have two simultaneous snakes (green P1 and orange or blue P2), a dark HUD with per-player scores, an overlay start menu with modes 1/2/3, and a game-over overlay. All restart on a keypress (R, Enter or Space) and use a shared collision model: walls, bodies, head-on, and any death ends the round. All use the same CPU recipe, BFS or greedy chase toward food with flood-fill fallback. The differences are mostly cosmetic or secondary. Attempt 1 has 3 foods and pause. Attempt 2 has P1 on WASD and a menu cursor. Attempt 3 uses a scoring heuristic with a capped flood-fill. Attempt 4 uses setInterval and a BFS+flood-fill AI. Attempt 5 has a pause, a checkerboard background and the weakest AI, a greedy Manhattan chase that treats tails as blocked. Attempt 6 only restarts with Enter or Space. Key assignments (arrows vs WASD for P1) and palettes also vary. These are minor feature and AI-sophistication differences, not different architectures or any attempt being broken.

All six attempts use the same core approach: a single-file HTML/CSS/JavaScript canvas game with a 30×30 grid, two snakes, food, three human/CPU mode combinations, score display, and menu/game-over controls. The implementations differ in visual styling and some details, such as one attempt supporting multiple food items and others using one, but their structure and overall completeness are comparable across attempts.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with a dat.gui panel, one 800×800 canvas and the required palette. The sections run in the same order: setup, GUI, growth, synapses, pulses, render. Every attempt uses random-walk branches drawn with quadratic smoothing, with synapses and spark pulses between tips, and has regenerate, clear and pause buttons. Quality and implementation details vary, though. I read the code for attempts 1 and 2 and compared the screenshots for all six.

- **Growth model:** Attempt 1 redraws every branch each frame from stored point lists. Attempt 2 draws segments onto a persistent offscreen layer. The shots look very different as a result.
- **Network density:** In shot 2 the tangle is dense and overgrown, and the pink synapses are mostly lost in it. Shots 3 and 4 show sparse networks, and shot 3 shows tiny, still-growing fragments with little synapse activity. Shot 5 is sparse and split into two clusters. Shot 6 is a rich, well-formed network.
- **Pulse and synapse logic:** Attempt 1 hops pulses along a branch adjacency map. Attempt 2 hops to any synapse within 70px. Synapses are drawn as a visible pink line plus a dot in attempt 1, and as a faint line (alpha 0.12) with a dot in attempt 2.
- **GUI labels and layout:** Attempt 1 uses the full descriptive names ("branch growth speed", "distance threshold") and puts the buttons at the top level. Attempt 2 leaves the labels as raw camelCase and adds an extra 'Actions' folder. Shots 4 and 5 also show camelCase labels, while shot 6 has shortened names such as 'pulseBright'. The scanline and vignette treatments differ too, and the title and HUD placement varies from attempt to attempt.
- **Stopping growth:** Attempt 1 grows continuously until it hits the branch cap, while attempt 2 stops once all tips are done.

The approach is consistent, but visual quality and completeness are noticeably variable between attempts.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a single canvas with dat.gui controls, branching neon neurons, synapses, and animation. The results vary substantially in visual quality and density: attempt 03 shows a tiny, cramped network in the canvas center; attempt 02 is an overcrowded tangle; attempt 01 is sparse with conspicuous straight magenta connections; attempts 04 and 05 produce clearer, more balanced networks; and attempt 06 is much denser and more polished. The implementation approach is consistent, but the rendered outcomes are not comparable in quality.

All six attempts take the same approach. Each is a single HTML file of 75–91 KB. They share the same dark gold-on-black palette, a Georgia serif headline with an italic gold "Reimagined", a pill-shaped gold CTA, and the same badge, scroll-cue and sticky-nav treatment. I only read the screenshots for attempts 1, 3 and 5, and I did not open the HTML files, so I have not checked the 8 artist cards, the modals, the .ics code or the SVG map in any attempt.

The hero, the first thing a visitor sees, varies a lot in those three. Attempt 1 has a dim museum-interior background with a three-photo collage on the right. The collage includes an off-theme beach and palm-tree photo and a large blank white panel, which looks like a mismatched image. Attempt 3 has no visible hero image at all, only a near-black spotlight gradient with left-aligned text, so it looks flatter and less cinematic. This may be an image that failed to load. Attempt 5 has a full-bleed, saturated abstract painting behind the text, with the navbar showing a "MUSEUM NIGHT" sub-label and an icon-based date/time/place chip row.

The hero layout, the imagery, the navbar details and the metadata badges all differ. That means the visual quality and how well the Unsplash images render are uneven from one attempt to the next. Because the approach is consistent but the quality is variable, I rate it 0.5.

The attempts share a recognizable dark, gold-accented ARTIFACT landing-page approach and all screenshots show a designed hero with event details and ticket/calendar calls to action. Quality and execution vary: attempt 01 uses an editorial collage but includes an obviously irrelevant beach image; attempts 02 and 03 have sparse, nearly empty black hero backgrounds; attempts 04–06 use full-bleed images, but 04's landscape is unrelated to a museum and 06 uses a close-up texture. The artifact counts also vary, with artist-card matches ranging from 6 to 22 and image tags from 3 to 13. Overall the concept is consistent, but visual quality and completeness are uneven across attempts.

All six attempts took the same approach, and I judge their quality as comparable. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with a 600x600 canvas, a 30x30 grid of 20px cells, and menu, game-over and pause overlays. Each uses the same two-snake design (green and blue, with a CPU snake as one or both) in three modes: human vs human, CPU vs human and CPU vs CPU. Controls are WASD for one snake and the arrow keys for the other, with 1/2/3 to pick a mode and R or Enter to restart. The CPU AI is the same in every attempt: BFS to the food, with flood-fill-based survival logic as a fallback. The scores sit in a HUD above the board, and the screenshots show a dark theme with a matching glowing design. I read attempts 1 and 2 in full and only grepped 3–6 for structure and AI logic. They are not identical. Attempts 1 and 6 drive the game with a requestAnimationFrame accumulator, while attempt 2 uses setInterval. HUD layouts differ (chips, panels, or score and length cards). The restart and menu keys also differ (R/Enter, R/M or R/Enter/Space). Attempt 3 adds a tail-chasing AI fallback. These are stylistic and minor variations, and I saw no sign of a broken or half-finished attempt, so quality varies little.

All six attempts build a polished, single-file two-snake game with the same three modes, CPU play, score display, and menu flow, so the overall implementation quality is broadly comparable. They vary substantially in presentation and structure: the screenshots show several distinct menu and HUD layouts, and the code uses different game-state and AI implementations. The results are consistently complete at a high level, but they do not follow the same specific approach.

All six attempts produce a working Canvas 2D cube with the same core features: rotation matrices, perspective projection, backface culling, quads split into triangles, per-vertex Lambert lighting, a moving light, W and P toggles, and an FPS readout. The screenshots I viewed (attempts 1 and 3) are both clean, plausible renders. I only read attempts 1–3 in full. For 4–6 I checked only which Canvas calls they use. The rasterization approach diverges, though. Attempt 1 draws no per-pixel Gouraud. It fills each triangle with a Canvas linearGradient that reproduces the affine intensity field, and it draws to the canvas directly at DPR up to 2. Attempts 2 and 3, and from the grep also 4, 5 and 6, write pixels into an ImageData buffer with a software scanline rasterizer and call putImageData. Attempt 5 appears to use a separate lower-resolution buffer (VW, VH). Implementation details also differ:
- **Attempt 2** interpolates RGB colors and uses painter's-algorithm depth sorting.
- **Attempt 3** interpolates intensity, adds distance attenuation and clamping, forces the normal outward, and exposes test hooks on globalThis.
- **HUD:** attempt 1 uses a DOM text overlay, attempt 2 a styled DOM panel with clickable chips, and attempt 3 draws the HUD on the canvas.
- **Wireframe:** attempt 1 and attempt 3 cull back-facing quads, while attempt 2 overlays the diagonals on the solid render.
- **Visual style:** cube colors and light paths differ, as do the render look and the HUD richness.

No attempt is broken, so quality is broadly comparable. Structure and technique vary enough (gradient trick versus scanline, different HUDs, extras) that this is consistent in intent but variable in execution.

All six attempt a rotating Canvas 2D cube with an FPS display and W/P controls, but their implementations and results vary. They use different shading and rasterization approaches, and the screenshots range from reasonably clear cubes to oversized flat faces; attempt 05 shows only one dark face. The shared task structure is consistent, but quality is uneven.

All six attempts use the same approach: a single HTML file with vanilla JS in an IIFE, a `todos` array plus a filter variable, and a full `render()` that rebuilds the list with createElement/textContent. I read the code but did not run any of them, and I did not open the screenshots. Reading the code, I found no functional bug in any attempt, so all six should meet the five requirements. The differences are cosmetic or minor extras. Attempt 3 adds a gradient background and round toggles, and puts new todos at the top with `unshift` instead of appending. Attempts 2 and 6 add 'Clear completed'. Attempt 6 also persists the selected filter and uses event delegation with a footer-based layout. Attempts 4 and 5 use a click handler instead of a form submit, and attempt 4 labels its delete button 'Delete' instead of '×'. The storage key and the completion field name (`done` in attempt 2, `completed` elsewhere) also vary. None of this changes the architecture or the quality level.

All six use the same basic single-page approach: add todos, toggle completion, delete items, filter the list, and save todos in localStorage. They differ noticeably in layout and styling, and in implementation details such as separate empty-state displays, optional clear-completed controls, and whether the filter is persisted. Quality is mostly comparable, but attempts 01 and 06 show a garbled delete symbol, while attempt 06 toggles completion when clicking anywhere on a todo row. These differences suggest a consistent approach with some variation in polish and behavior.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with a canvas, dat.gui loaded from cdnjs, and the four folders Growth, Synapses, Pulses and Visuals. Attempt 1 is a dense, bright network with hundreds of synapses. Attempt 2 is a moderate tree-like network with a visible scanline band. Attempt 3 is a small, tidy cluster. It loads dat.gui from `dat.gui/0.7.9` while the others use `dat-gui/0.7.9`, which likely breaks the load, though I did not confirm that. The GUI layout differs too: some attempts have collapsed folders and some have extra controls. The structure is consistent, but quality ranges from rich to broken.

All six attempts use the same broad approach: a self-contained HTML canvas simulation with dat.gui controls, procedural branching, neon colors, and animated signals. All six attempts take the same basic approach. All six attempts follow the same overall structure and visual direction: a dark, gold-accented ARTIFACT landing page with a large serif hero, navigation, event details, and the requested event sections. I read attempts 01 and 02 in full and compared all six screenshots. I only grepped attempts 03–06 for key API calls, so the claims about their code are less certain. The approach is consistent. At least 01 and 02 are CPU software rasterizers that write per-pixel barycentric Gouraud fills into an ImageData/Uint32Array and blit with putImageData. Both use 8 shared vertices with averaged smooth normals, per-vertex Lambert lighting, a 3x3 rotation matrix, perspective projection, backface culling, a moving light with a glow marker, W/P toggles and an FPS readout. The screenshots suggest the others look similar: a 60 FPS HUD, a glowing light dot and 4–6 visible triangles. Quality and presentation vary noticeably. Attempt 01 has a perspective-correct depth buffer, a warm tint and a clearly visible smooth gradient across the faces. Attempt 02 shows a mostly dark blue face with a barely visible gradient. Attempt 03 shows a very dark, almost flat green face. Attempt 04 is dark with only a faint gradient on the green face and a bit more on the purple one. Attempt 05 draws a small cube inside a bordered 800x600 panel, and its light dot is clipped at the panel's bottom edge. Attempt 06 is the most vivid, with six saturated face colours and strong visible gradients. The HUD also differs a lot: canvas text in 01, a DOM panel in 02, 03 and 04, a one-line bar in 05, and multiple corner panels in 06. All are functional and none is broken. They differ in shading visibility, layout and polish, which makes this consistent approach with variable quality.

All six attempts use a Canvas 2D software-rendering approach with a rotating cube, FPS display, and wireframe/pause controls, so the overall approach is consistent. The cube size and HUD also vary noticeably, and the reported triangle counts differ.

I read attempts 01, 06 and part of 03 in full and viewed screenshots 01 and 02. I did not open attempts 02, 04 and 05 or shots 03–06, so the rest rests on file sizes (13.7–18.9 KB). All six attempts use the same overall approach: a polished, dark-and-gold editorial landing page with the same major sections and interactions, including the program, artist cards, tickets, FAQ, newsletter, and calendar download. All six attempts use the same approach: a hand-written CPU rasterizer on a Canvas 2D ImageData buffer with a reciprocal-depth buffer and perspective-correct barycentric colour interpolation. The differences are in lighting and visual result, not in architecture. Attempts 1, 2 and 4 use smoothed corner normals (normalized vertex positions). Attempts 3, 5 and 6 use per-face normals with per-face base colours, and attempts 5 and 6 add hard edges and attenuation. Presentation also varies: fullscreen canvas (2, 6), card layout (1, 3, 5) and grid layout (4). Light handling varies too, with a light-behind-cube test in some and a light marker with a label in others. Output quality differs in the screenshots I viewed (1, 3 and 5). Attempt 1 shows a near-black, almost featureless green silhouette that doesn't read as a lit cube. Attempt 3 shows a clearly three-faced, smoothly shaded cube. Attempt 5 shows one large face with a gradient and a very dark side face. I didn't view screenshots 2, 4 or 6. So the approach is consistent but the visible result varies from weak to good.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a Canvas 2D software renderer with cube vertices and faces, triangle rasterization, rotation, lighting, FPS display, and W/P controls. All six attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with an 800×800 canvas, dat.gui with Growth/Synapses/Pulses/Visuals folders, neon cyan branches with yellow-green accents, magenta synapse dots, yellow pulse sparks, scanlines and a vignette. All six attempts take a broadly consistent approach: each is a single 800×800 canvas page with dat.gui, four named folders, neon palette values, and a requestAnimationFrame loop. All 6 attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single self-contained HTML file with vanilla JS and a render() function that rebuilds the list. Each has the same layout: a centered card with an Add form, All/Active/Completed filter buttons, a todo list and an items-left count. Attempts 1 and 4 also persist the active filter and the todo list as an object, while 2, 3, 5 and 6 store only a todos array. All six attempts use a single-file todo app with the same basic card, input, filters, checkbox completion, deletion, and localStorage pattern, but quality varies. Attempts 1, 4, and 5 have more robust state handling and clearer empty states; 2, 3, and 6 use a simpler array and `done` schema. Attempt 2's delete button renders corrupted characters, attempt 3 omits the clear-completed control, and attempt 6 puts a div directly inside the list. The screenshots show a broadly similar centered-card interface, but with noticeable styling differences, including attempt 6's saturated purple background and attempt 3's compact card. Overall the approach is consistent, with uneven implementation quality.

The six attempts share one approach and the same overall design language. Quality is not uniform, though, and the hero in particular varies a lot. I read the INSTRUCTIONS.md brief and the six hero screenshots. I only counted keyword matches across the HTML files, with no per-section comparison. I did not open the code or check the modals, .ics download, forms or console errors.

What is the same in every attempt:

- The navbar has the same links and a gold pill 'Get Tickets' button.

- Each has the 'ARTIFACT: Museum Night' eyebrow line, metadata chips or panels, and gold 'Get Tickets' and outlined 'Save to Calendar' CTAs.

All six attempts follow a similar structure and visual approach: a dark, gold-accented editorial landing page with a large serif hero, event details, timeline, artist area, tickets, FAQ, newsletter, and JavaScript interactions. The screenshots show a recognizable shared design, though the hero background varies from nearly plain dark (01, 04) to prominent imagery (02, 03, 05, 06).
