The artifacts otherwise repeatedly include calendar-download, ticket, modal, and FAQ-related code, so the approach is consistent but execution and visual completeness vary between attempts.

All six attempts use the same approach: a CPU barycentric Gouraud rasterizer writing into an ImageData buffer, 3x3 rotation matrices, perspective projection, per-vertex Lambert lighting, a W/P key handler, an FPS counter in the HUD, and a light marker. Details differ. Geometry is 2 triangles per face in attempts 2 and 4, and a 6x6 or 8x8 grid per face in 1, 3, 5 and 6. Colour is a single orange base in 1, 2 and 6, and per-face colours in 3, 4 and 5. Culling is view-space in 1, face-normal in 2, 3 and 4, and screen-area in 5 and 6. Attempt 6 also adds a z-buffer. Quality varies noticeably. shot-02 shows a completely blank black canvas with no cube and no HUD, so attempt 2 looks broken. I could not find the cause when reading the code. shot-04 shows a clean, correctly shaded cube. shot-06 shows a very dark cube with a blurry orange blob, because its pure spherical normals make Lambert shading look unlike a cube. The shared structure points to one approach, but the output ranges from broken to clean to oddly shaded.

All six attempts follow the same broad Canvas 2D pipeline: rotating cube geometry, projected triangles, per-vertex lighting, a moving light, and W/P controls with FPS. Quality varies substantially. Attempts 01, 03, 05, and 06 use subdivided cube faces for visible Gouraud gradients; 02 and 04 use only corner vertices. Attempt 04’s perspective helper is unused and its wireframe loop mistakenly uses the first face’s triangles for every face. Attempt 02 also has malformed, fragile gradient-color construction in wireframe mode. Attempt 06 adds depth buffering, while 03 uses a packed pixel buffer. So the approach is recognizable across attempts, but implementation quality and rendering behavior are uneven.

All six attempts take the same approach. Each is a single HTML file with a canvas-based 30x30 grid. All six use the same basic approach: a centered canvas, dat.gui folders, animated branching neurons, glowing synapses, and neon colors. All six attempts take the same approach and reach about the same quality. Each is a single HTML file with the same dark-and-gold design. Each also has a scroll hint and a spotlight overlay. A keyword count shows the same features in every file: 'View details' buttons, the .ics calendar code and IntersectionObserver scroll reveal. The counts are 7, 6, 6, 7, 7 and 7 across attempts 1–6, so attempts 2 and 3 each have one fewer match than the rest. The differences I saw are small. The hero background image varies, because the Unsplash source returns random photos: a city skyline in attempts 1 and 2, a Louvre-style building in 4, a meadow in 5, and no visible photo in 3 and 6. Attempts 4 and 5 add a side highlights card, and the badge sets differ slightly. In the screenshots, attempts 1 and 5 have hero text flush against the left edge with less padding. I did not open the artifacts in a browser, so I did not test the modals, forms or console errors.

All six attempts follow a recognizable shared approach: a single-file, dark-and-gold editorial landing page with the same oversized serif hero, event metadata, ticket and calendar buttons, and the same eight broad sections. The screenshots show comparable premium styling overall, though the hero imagery and layout vary substantially, including cityscape, Louvre, open field, and mostly abstract backgrounds. The implementations also vary in completeness: artist-card markers range from 2 in attempt 03 to 25 in attempt 06, and FAQ markers from 0 in attempt 06 to 13 in attempts 04 and 05. Each artifact has a modal, inline SVG, and calendar-related code, and all six include six FAQ question texts, but the structural-marker differences suggest uneven implementation. This is a consistent general approach with noticeable variation in quality and execution.

All five attempts take the same approach. Each is a single HTML file with a 600x600 canvas, a 30x30 grid, a requestAnimationFrame loop and a dark neon UI. Each is a two-snake game with the three modes (human vs human, cpu vs human, cpu vs cpu), a start menu, score panels for both players, a pause key and Esc to return to the menu. Each has a game-over overlay and restarts with R or Space. The CPU AI uses the same technique everywhere: BFS or greedy pathfinding to the food, plus flood-fill safety checks (BFS in attempts 2 and 3, greedy with flood-fill in 1, 4 and 5). The screenshots show start menus with the same three mode buttons and a score bar above the board. The differences are cosmetic: titles, accent colours, a speed selector in attempt 2, and which player gets WASD versus the arrow keys. I did not run the games, so this rests on reading the code structure and screenshots. Quality looks comparable across all five.

The attempts share a consistent overall design: all five are single-file canvas games on a 30×30 grid, with three mode buttons, two snakes, score displays, CPU steering, and menu/game-over overlays. Their quality varies in important behavior. Attempts 1, 2, and 4 end games when a snake dies in the human modes; attempt 5 ends only when both snakes are dead, so a surviving snake can continue after the other crashes. Attempt 3 also reverses which snake is CPU-controlled in CPU-vs-human compared with the other attempts. Restart keys and pause behavior differ, and attempts 2–5 use different CPU pathfinding strategies. These are meaningful inconsistencies, but the artifacts remain recognizably the same game rather than divergent implementations.

All six attempts take the same approach. Each is a single HTML file with a Canvas 2D software rasterizer: 8 cube vertices, 6 quads split into 12 triangles, 3x3 rotation matrices, perspective projection and screen-space backface culling. Each does per-vertex Lambert lighting with normals taken as the normalized corner direction, barycentric or edge-function Gouraud interpolation into a Uint32 ImageData buffer, a moving point light with a drawn marker, W and P key handlers, and an FPS readout. The screenshots show the same look: a dark background, a lit cube with per-face colors, a HUD at top left and 60 FPS. Quality and details vary between attempts. (1) Attempts 1, 2, 4 and 6 use a z-buffer. Attempts 3 and 5 have none and rely on culling alone, which is adequate for a convex cube. (2) Attempts 1 and 5 render at full resolution, attempts 2, 3 and 4 at half resolution, and attempt 6 at a fixed 640x480 with letterboxing (the black side bars in its screenshot). (3) Attempts 3 and 5 interpolate color without perspective correction. Attempt 2 interpolates it perspective-correct, and attempts 1, 4 and 6 do not. (4) Attempt 3 lights with the face normal rather than the smoothed vertex normals and adds distance attenuation. (5) W toggles wireframe in most attempts but cycles through three modes in attempt 4. Attempt 6 draws vertex dots in wireframe. (6) The HUD differs: plain text overlays in most, a canvas-drawn panel in attempts 4 and 6. (7) Attempt 6 has the most polished handling of light occlusion, the top-left fill rule and the background gradient, while attempt 5 is minimal. (8) Several screenshots are very dark, with only parts of the cube lit. This reflects light placement and ambient choices that vary across attempts. The shared architecture is stable, but features, polish and lighting results differ noticeably, so this is consistent approach with variable quality.

All six attempts use the same basic Canvas 2D software-rendering approach: a rotating cube built from vertices and split faces, with lighting, FPS, and W/P controls. Quality varies substantially. Attempts 1–3 and 5 show very dark, simple cubes; attempt 4 adds a more polished framebuffer, background, and HUD; attempt 6 uses another detailed rasterizer but its screenshot shows essentially one visible face. The shared structure is consistent, but the results are not comparable in quality.

All six attempts use the same approach: a single self-contained HTML file with vanilla JS in an IIFE, an array of {id, text, completed}, a render() that rebuilds the list, and a try/catch load/save to localStorage. Each one meets every requirement: add (button and/or Enter), checkbox toggle with line-through, delete, All/Active/Completed filter, and persistence. Each also adds the same extras: an items-left counter, a Clear completed button, and empty-state messages. Quality is comparable and no attempt looks broken. The differences are cosmetic or minor. Visual styling varies (attempt 1 is a plain light-grey card; 2–6 use the purple gradient card). Some attempts use a <form> submit (1, 2, 5) and others use a button click plus keydown (3, 4, 6). Event handling is delegated in 2 and 3 and attached per element in the rest. Attempts 2 and 6 also persist the active filter. The localStorage key names differ, and attempt 4's key is the odd 'todos.openrouter-deepseek'. Attempt 4 also lacks a disabled state on Clear completed. I judged none of these differences to affect function or overall quality.

All six attempts use a self-contained vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript todo app with localStorage, add/complete/delete actions, and All/Active/Completed filters, so the overall approach is consistent. Quality varies: attempts 01, 04, and 06 have recognizable delete controls, while attempts 02 and 05 contain replacement or corrupted glyphs for controls or empty-state icons. The storage format and interaction structure also vary across attempts, and attempt 03 uses a different DOM structure and storage key. These differences make the results less consistent in polish and implementation details.

All six attempts follow the same broad approach: one HTML file, dat.gui from a CDN, an 800×800 canvas, the neon palette, and growth, synapse, pulse and render sections. The implementation details and the output quality vary a lot. In attempt 1, each branch is a single precomputed quadratic Bézier that is revealed over time. Neurons are glowing orbs and synapses are radial-gradient blobs. The GUI is restyled with a custom CSS theme and all controls are visible. In attempt 2, branches are random-walk point lists drawn with quadraticCurveTo midpoints. It has a grid and a caption, and the GUI is default-styled and collapsed. In shot 2 the branches are clumped near the center. Attempt 3 adds a status/HUD text overlay ('STATUS: STABLE, NODES, SYNAPSES'). It has a different GUI style, includes extra 'background glow' controls, and shows sparse, fragmented branches. Attempt 4 renders thin, spiky, tangled branches with heavy accent-colored yellow-green clusters. Its GUI buttons are named 'regenerate', 'clearCanvas' and 'pause / resume', so they differ from the spec wording used elsewhere. Attempt 5 puts the controls in an extra 'Actions' folder, which is another structure. Its shot shows mostly yellow-green branches with no visible synapses or pulses, so the synapse and pulse requirements look unmet. Shot 6 shows only scattered dots and tiny fragments, with no coherent branch network, so it looks broken or stalled early. The visible results range from a polished glowing network (1) to an almost empty canvas (6). That is a consistent overall approach with clearly variable quality and details, so I rate it 0.5.

The attempts diverge substantially in structure and visible results. Attempt 01 draws smooth quadratic branches with a dense scanline treatment, while 02 uses point-based growth and a grid; 06 grows branches incrementally with wobble. Their screenshots also range from a compact glowing network (01–02) to faint sparse branches (03), a dense angular tangle (04), a few isolated strands (05), and a tiny, disconnected cluster (06). GUI layouts and visual treatments vary as well, so the results are not comparable across attempts.

I judged this from the six hero screenshots only. I did not open the HTML files, because my file-inspection command was blocked. All six attempts share one approach: a single dark-gold cinematic page with a sticky navbar (ARTIFACT logo, Program/Artists/Venue/Tickets/FAQ, gold Get Tickets button). The hero has a large Georgia-style serif headline 'Museum Night, Reimagined', a gold event-name eyebrow, date/time/place pills, and Get Tickets plus Save to Calendar CTAs. Each hero also has a 'Scroll' cue. The palette is near-black with a gold accent in every attempt. The differences are cosmetic: attempt 1 has a plain non-italic headline and no scroll cue; attempts 2–6 italicise 'Reimagined' in gold; attempts 3, 4 and 6 use pill-shaped buttons; attempt 5 has square buttons and a bordered nav CTA; attempt 2 has extra badges ('After hours', '18+'); the left offset varies (about 50px to 230px). Only attempt 4 shows a broken-image alt-text artifact, which comes from the remote Unsplash hero image failing to load, so it is probably an environment effect and not a quality gap. Overall the polish and design level are comparable, with no attempt visibly broken or much weaker.

All six attempts use a similar dark, gold-accented editorial layout with a sticky navigation, oversized serif hero, event metadata, and ticket/calendar calls to action, and each includes the main single-page sections and interaction concepts. Quality and completeness vary: shot 04 visibly has a broken hero image, while shots 01, 05, and 06 show mostly empty dark hero areas; shots 02 and 03 have more coherent, polished hero compositions. The files also differ in coverage: FAQ markers range from 2 to 13, and some attempts have seven sections while others have eight. They follow a consistent approach, but the visual and implementation quality is uneven.

All six attempts use the same approach: a hand-written software rasterizer. Each one does per-vertex Lambert lighting, interpolates colour across split triangles, and writes pixels into an ImageData buffer shown with putImageData. Each has mat3 rotations, perspective projection, backface culling, W/P keys, an FPS readout and an orbiting light, and the code is structured near-identically (resize, mat3Mul/rotX/rotY, project, rasterizeTriangle, render, loop). Quality and visual result vary noticeably, judging from the screenshots and a grep of attempts 2–6; I read only attempt 1 in full. Attempt 1 has the camera so close that the cube overflows the viewport, with a large near-black face and a clipped red top. Attempt 5 also zooms in, so a single purple face fills most of the screen. Attempt 3 is rendered in a bordered square canvas, with a very dark, muddy cube that shows 'tris: 4'. Attempts 2 and 4 show a well-framed cube with clear shading and a clean HUD. Attempt 6 shows a mid-size cube with a bright lit face. The HUD styles, framing, scale and lighting contrast differ from run to run, so the framing and visible shading quality are inconsistent.

All six attempts use a self-contained Canvas 2D software-rendering pipeline for a rotating, lit cube and include FPS plus W/P controls, so the approach is broadly consistent. The results vary substantially: attempt 01 shows a severely oversized, clipped cube; attempt 03 confines a dim cube to a smaller framed canvas; attempt 05 renders a small cube; and attempts 04 and 06 show much larger cubes. Attempt 02 is more balanced, though its visible faces look mostly flat. These differences make the quality inconsistent across attempts.

All six attempts use the same approach. Each is a single HTML file with a 600x600 canvas for a 30x30 grid and a setInterval or tick game loop. In each, the CPU snake uses BFS to the food with a flood-fill safety fallback. Each has the three modes (human vs human, human vs CPU, CPU vs CPU), a start menu, a score display, a game over screen and a restart key. I read the start-menu screenshots for attempts 1, 4 and 6 (a dark neon UI with three mode choices and WASD/arrow controls) and confirmed the shared structure for the rest by searching the code. I did not run the games or read every attempt in full, so I cannot confirm that gameplay quality is equal. The differences are cosmetic or extras: file size (23–40 KB), branding (Cyber Snake, Snake Battle, Snake Arena), and extras such as a speed selector, sound and high score in attempt 6. Structure and apparent quality are comparable across all six.

All six attempts use the same overall approach: a single HTML file with a canvas-based 30×30 arena, a start menu for the three play modes, score display, keyboard controls, and CPU movement based on pathfinding. The screenshots show consistently polished, complete menus with clear controls and matching dark arcade styling. The presentation and extras vary—such as speed selection in attempts 3 and 6, and pause or audio features in some attempts—but none appears structurally or qualitatively divergent.

I read attempts 01, 04 and 06 in full and checked the screenshots for 01 and 05. I did not open attempts 02, 03 and 05 or the screenshots for 02, 03, 04 and 06. The three attempts I read take the same approach. Each is a single self-contained HTML file in vanilla JS with a `todos` array and a `render()` function that rebuilds the list. Each saves to localStorage on every change and filters through a `currentFilter` variable. Each uses the same indigo/slate design tokens, a card layout, and an Add form with All/Active/Completed buttons. Each has strikethrough on completed items, per-item delete, an 'items left' counter and Clear completed. All three appear to meet every requirement. The differences are cosmetic or minor: the titles differ (Todos, Tasks, Task Tracker; shot-05 shows Task Manager). Attempt 06 and the shot-05 attempt have a dark theme. Attempt 04 persists the selected filter. Attempt 06 uses event delegation and try/catch around storage. Attempts 04 and 06 use custom checkboxes and SVG icons. The file sizes of about 9–13 KB are similar. None of these is a functional gap, and I saw no broken attempt, so quality is comparable and the approach is the same.

All six attempts use the same basic structure: a single-page todo app with a form, completion checkboxes, delete controls, three filters, and localStorage. Their presentation varies considerably: attempts 1 and 3 use light cards, attempt 2 uses a dark theme, attempt 5 uses a dark full-card layout, and attempt 6 adds system-based dark mode and a different card layout. Quality is broadly comparable, though attempt 2 has a malformed checkbox checkmark CSS rule, while attempts 4–6 add stronger handling such as saved filters or guarded storage parsing. The consistent implementation approach with visible quality and design variation fits 0.5.

All five attempts take the same basic approach: a single HTML file with a canvas, dat.gui from a CDN, and branch, synapse and pulse arrays, with growth, synapse and pulse logic and a vignette. Quality varies a lot, though. Attempt 1 is a dense, clean network with all requested controls and synapses only at a few spots. Attempt 2 grows sparse, mostly yellow, directional bundles, and its pulses look like big beaded blobs. Attempt 3 is the most polished: a clean, well-balanced network with a proper control panel. Attempt 4 shows an empty Visuals folder, so the colour controls are missing, has a teal-washed background that breaks the #05070f palette, and has a huge yellow pulse blob. Attempt 5 produces a synapse explosion that covers the scene in magenta clutter. The structure is shared, but the output ranges from good (3) to visibly broken or non-compliant (4, 5, and to a lesser extent 2).

All five attempts use the same general approach: a single canvas, dat.gui folders for growth, synapses, pulses, and visuals, and animated branching networks with synapse and pulse effects. Their quality varies noticeably, though. Attempt 1 has a dense central network; attempt 2 grows into four separated arms; attempt 3 spreads a finer network across the canvas; attempt 4 has an overbright teal background and blown-out yellow clusters; and attempt 5 is crowded with glowing magenta connections. The shared structure is consistent, but the visual results are not comparable in polish or readability.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single dark, gold-accented HTML file with a Georgia serif headline, an italic gold 'Reimagined', the same nav links, and a gold 'Get Tickets' button plus 'Save to Calendar'. The code-level checks I ran show all six contain the required pieces (the 'View details' buttons, inline SVG, and a text/calendar Blob for the .ics download). The structure is the same, but the hero layout and styling vary a lot, and image quality is uneven. 1) Attempts 1 and 2 use a full-bleed dark background image, left-aligned. Attempt 1 has a bordered metadata box and badges, and attempt 2 has a subtitle and an inline-icon metadata row. 2) Attempt 3 has no hero image, with a centred-left text block, dotted grain and pill badges. 3) Attempts 4 and 5 use a split hero with an image card on the right. Attempt 4's image is an irrelevant construction-crane photo, and attempt 5 uses an abstract painting and a noticeably burgundy background. Attempt 5 also adds an extra 'About' nav link, so its nav differs from the specified one. 4) Attempt 6 has a fully centred hero with no image and a feature-tag row. Because source.unsplash.com is unreliable, the hero image outcomes differ widely between attempts: dark but plausible, none, a mismatched crane photo, and an abstract painting. Visual polish and the closeness to the 'velvet dark' palette also vary. Quality is broadly comparable and none looks broken, but the layouts and visual results differ enough to call this consistent approach with variable results, not full stability.

All six attempts use the same broad premium, dark-and-gold museum-night direction, with a serif hero headline and ticket and calendar calls to action. Their visual executions vary noticeably: attempts 1 and 4 use left-and-right split heroes with prominent images; 5 also uses a split layout but shifts to a much brighter red palette and abstract artwork; 2 is left-aligned over a dark background; 3 centers the hero; and 6 uses a compact centered text layout without a visible hero image. The screenshots show a consistent concept, but differing composition and visual quality make the results variable rather than closely comparable.

The five attempts diverge in architecture and in what they actually show. They share one broad idea: a software rasterizer that writes into a pixel buffer and puts it on the canvas. Everything below that differs, and the screenshots range from a working cube to blank canvases.

Structure and shading:
- Attempts 1, 2 and 4 share 8 corner vertices, normals taken from the normalized vertex position, and z-buffering. Attempt 5 also uses the 8-corner normals but has no z-buffer.
- Attempt 3 uses 24 per-face vertices with true face normals, distance attenuation and a different rotation-matrix setup.
- Attempt 2 is the only one that fills the whole window, with a resizing canvas (up to 800x600).
- Attempt 5 uses a square 640x640 canvas.

Rasterizer:
- Attempts 1, 3 and 4 use barycentric rasterizers. Attempts 3 and 4 add perspective-correct interpolation.
- Attempts 2 and 5 use scanline rasterizers.
- Attempt 5 uses painter's sorting and no depth test.

Features:
- Wireframe is drawn with canvas strokes in attempts 1, 2 and 5, but with a Bresenham line into the pixel buffer in attempts 3 and 4.
- Attempts 3 and 5 add Space to pause. Attempt 5 adds on-screen buttons. Attempts 4 and 5 add mouse drag rotation.
- Attempt 5 uses fixed per-frame rotation increments rather than dt-based ones.

Output quality in the screenshots:
- Attempt 1 shows a recognizable multicolor cube with a smooth gradient.
- Attempt 2 shows a multicolor face and a light marker, but the cube silhouette looks malformed and the lighting is very dark.
- Attempt 3 shows an empty canvas with no cube. Its backface-culling sign looks wrong.
- Attempt 4 shows a flat dark-green blob, not a shaded cube. It has a bug in the blue-channel shading (the color variable `b0` is shadowed by the barycentric `b0`). It also reuses the z-buffer incorrectly.
- Attempt 5 shows an empty black canvas.

Across attempts, quality ranges from clearly working to completely blank, and the implementation choices differ widely. That is divergent and random.

All five attempts use a similar Canvas 2D cube pipeline with rotating geometry, Gouraud lighting, wireframe and pause controls, and FPS display, but the rendered results vary substantially. Attempts 1 and 2 show a clearly visible shaded cube; attempt 4 shows a very dark cube; attempts 3 and 5 show no visible cube in their screenshots. The consistent approach but uneven visible outcomes indicate variable quality across attempts.

I read attempts 01, 03 and 05 in full and looked at screenshots 03 and 05. I did not open 02, 04 or 06, and their file sizes (6.6–7.6 KB) are in the same range. All the attempts I read use the same approach: one vanilla-JS HTML file with an in-file `<style>`, a `todos` array and `currentFilter` state, `save`/`load` through localStorage, and a full re-render on every change. Each one covers every requirement: add (button and Enter), toggle with line-through, delete, All/Active/Completed filter buttons, and persistence. Each also has an empty-state message and trims input. The differences are cosmetic or minor. 03 uses a purple gradient card with pill filters and a hover-only Delete button. 01 and 05 use a plain grey page with a segmented filter bar. 05 uses a native checkbox and a form submit, and it has no item counter. The localStorage key differs (`todos`, `todos_app_data`, or a model-specific key). 01 builds the DOM with createElement, while 03 and 05 use innerHTML with escapeHtml. 03 uses inline `onclick` handlers, so its functions have to be global. 05 reads localStorage without a try/catch. None of these is a functional gap. Quality is comparable and nothing is broken, so the attempts are stable.

All six attempts use the same basic single-page todo pattern with add, filter, completion, deletion, and localStorage, and most appear broadly functional. Quality and implementation vary: attempts 1, 2, and 5 use direct per-item handlers; attempts 3, 4, and 6 use inline or delegated click handling. Attempt 4 identifies todos by their text, so duplicate tasks can target the wrong item, while attempt 6 toggles completion when clicking anywhere on a row and has no visible checkbox. Several files also contain garbled characters in headings or icons. These differences show a consistent overall approach but variable polish and behavior.

The attempts share one broad approach but differ in quality. All six build a single-file canvas game on a 30x30 grid with two competing snakes. They all have an overlay start menu, a score display and a game-over screen. The differences are mainly in the three attempts I read in full (1, 2 and 6). Attempts 3-5 I only compared by pattern counts, so the same differences likely apply to them. Attempt 1 uses BFS pathfinding, a setInterval tick, arrow-key menu navigation and a Space-to-menu restart. Attempt 2 uses a frame-count loop, a side scoreboard and a card-style menu. Its `cpuMove` greedy AI is never called, so the CPU snakes cannot steer, which breaks two of the three required modes. Attempt 6 uses BFS in an accumulator-based rAF loop, with a mode-button row under the canvas. It also has a dead first `gameTick` with a `snake2.head[i]` typo that a later override masks, and a clumsy Start Game flow. The CPU side also varies. In attempt 6 the CPU is snake 1, while in attempt 2 snake 1 is always human. Controls are inconsistent too: WASD for P1 and arrows for P2 in attempt 1, but WASD and arrows both for P1 and IJKL for P2 in attempts 2 and 6. The screenshots show different layouts and colour schemes, and the mode-selection UX differs. Quality ranges from a working BFS CPU (1, 6) to a non-functional CPU (2), so the approach is consistent but the quality is variable.

All six attempts use a JavaScript canvas game on a 30×30 grid, with two snakes, the three requested modes, score displays, menus, and CPU movement. Their overall approach is consistent, but the presentation and implementation quality vary: the screenshots show markedly different layouts and visual styles, and the source uses different game loops and CPU strategies. Some attempts also contain rough edges, such as corrupted title text in attempts 1, 3, and 6, and a snake-collision typo in attempt 6’s original gameTick code.

All five attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with Georgia serif headlines, a gold-italic 'Reimagined.', a dark velvet/burgundy palette, a sticky navbar with a gold 'Get Tickets' CTA, and meta badges for date, time and venue. Each has the same Get Tickets and Save to Calendar buttons. The details differ from attempt to attempt. The hero layout varies: attempt 1 is text-only left-aligned, attempt 2 is full-width with badge boxes, attempt 3 is centered, and attempts 4 and 5 are a split layout with an image slot on the right. The nav CTA style also varies, filled in attempts 1 and 3 and outlined in attempts 2 and 5. Attempt 3's nav CTA text is almost illegible, and attempt 4's is too. Remote Unsplash images are broken in the screenshots of attempts 2 to 5, which leaves a visibly broken hero image area; this is most obvious in attempts 4 and 5. Attempt 1 shows no image at all. File sizes also differ, from about 1340 lines (attempt 2) to about 2220 lines (attempt 4). The attempts generate artist cards in different ways: 'View details' appears literally only in attempts 2, 3 and 5. So the approach and design language are consistent, but polish and hero rendering vary noticeably between attempts.

All five attempts converge on the same dark, gold-accented editorial landing page, with the same main sections and broadly similar hero treatment. Their completeness and execution vary: attempts 2 and 3 include working-looking calendar, ticket and artist modal markup, while attempt 1 has only 5 FAQ entries and very little modal/calendar support; attempt 4 uses a substantially different program structure and has sparse interaction support; attempt 5 has more interaction code but no newsletter form. The screenshots also show broken or missing hero images in attempts 2, 4 and 5. This is a consistent overall approach with meaningful quality variation, rather than stable comparable results or wholly divergent attempts.

All six attempts use Canvas 2D with a hand-written software rasterizer, but their quality is wildly different and the structures diverge. Attempt 1 draws a blank canvas in the screenshot. Its `vsub` is called with four arguments, so the light vector is wrong. Pausing also stops the requestAnimationFrame loop, so it can never resume. Attempt 6 never resets `depthBuf`, so after the first frame only a few orange fragments remain, and the screenshot shows scattered slivers instead of a cube. Attempt 3 renders a cube-like orange shape with visible Gouraud gradients, but it is a mangled pentagon-like shape with no clear cube faces. It also has a depth-buffer quirk and an unused painter's-algorithm comment. Attempts 2, 4 and 5 differ again: attempt 2 uses ImageData with a depth buffer, attempt 4 uses a full-window canvas with painter's sorting and a perspective camera, and attempt 5 uses a z-buffer, extra R/Space keys and `preventDefault` on every key. Structure, HUD, canvas size, shading method (flat face normals vs averaged vertex normals), culling method, depth handling and FPS display all vary. Outcomes range from blank or broken to partly working, so the attempts are neither the same approach nor comparable quality.

The attempts diverge in both implementation and visible result. Screenshots 01 and 02 show empty canvases; 03 shows a small, nearly flat-shaded cube; 04 shows a broad, distorted slab; 05 is empty; and 06 shows only a few disconnected fragments. Their rendering approaches also vary, from scanline rasterization to barycentric software rasterizers and face-based drawing. The results are inconsistent, and most do not visibly deliver the requested rotating Gouraud-shaded cube.

I judged this from the six menu screenshots plus a keyword search of the files. I did not read the full source of any attempt or run any of the games. All six attempts look like the same solution: a single-file neon or terminal-style Snake game on a dark theme. Each has a start menu with the same three modes (Human vs Human, CPU vs Human, CPU vs CPU), selectable with the 1/2/3 keys. Each shows a P1/P2 score readout. All use a WASD plus Arrow-key split for the two players and have an R-to-restart key. Attempts 1, 2, 5 and 6 also use Space, Esc or M for pause or menu. The keyword counts for CPU and keyboard-handling terms (bfs, flood, safe, keydown, Enter, Space) are similar across files, from 16 to 25 matches each. That suggests comparable CPU-pathing and input logic. The differences are cosmetic: the title text (attempt 6 says 'SNAKE BATTLE'), colour palette, font, and whether P1 uses WASD or the arrows. Attempt 3 gives P1 the arrow keys and attempt 4 offers a click option. These look like stylistic variation, and I saw no sign that any attempt is broken or missing a required feature. Approach and apparent quality are consistent.

All six attempts use a single-page canvas game with a 30×30 board, two snakes, three play modes, scores, a menu, and CPU movement, so the core approach is consistent. The implementations and polish vary: attempt 1 uses a fixed interval and one food item with pause controls; attempt 2 adds a countdown, multiple foods, and speed changes; attempts 3–5 use different layouts and loop/input designs; attempt 6 has a more elaborate CPU pathfinding and collision system. The screenshots show a broadly similar dark neon menu, but presentation and details differ enough to indicate variable quality rather than fully stable output.

I judged this from the six screenshots only. I did not open the HTML files, because my command to inspect them was rejected. The attempts look very different from one another, in both structure and quality.

- Attempt 1: a dense cyan and yellow branching tree with large saturated magenta blobs. The synapse glow is overwhelming and hides the branches. The GUI folders are collapsed.
- Attempt 2: a sparse set of straight lines with magenta blobs, on a yellowish canvas background that does not match #05070f. All folders are open, and the buttons sit at the bottom.
- Attempt 3: a few smooth curved branches radiating out, with small ring-shaped synapses. This is the closest to the intended look. The GUI has Pause/Resume as a checkbox.
- Attempt 4: a web of straight magenta synapse lines with a gradient background glow and a status text at the bottom. It has an extra Max Branches control, and the Regenerate button sits inside the Growth folder.
- Attempt 5: only a tiny magenta blob in the middle, so growth looks broken or stalled. Its GUI has a separate Actions folder.
- Attempt 6: a completely blank canvas with no GUI, so it looks broken or failed to load.

The rendering approach differs (branch trees versus line webs versus almost nothing), the GUI layout differs, and quality ranges from working to blank. That is divergent and unstable.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a single canvas, dat.gui controls, and a neon neuron-growth simulation. Quality varies substantially: attempts 2–4 show animated branching networks, though their visuals differ (attempt 3 is sparse and attempt 4 is dominated by dense synapse lines); attempt 1 is an overly bright, tangled mass. Attempts 5 and 6 appear broken in the screenshots: 5 shows only a few glowing seed points, and 6 is blank. That points to a consistent approach with highly variable results.

All 6 attempts take the same approach: one self-contained HTML file with vanilla JS and inline CSS. Each uses the localStorage key 'todos', stores todos as {id, text, completed}, and rebuilds the list with a render() function that sets list.innerHTML = ''. Each implements add, complete with strikethrough, delete, and All/Active/Completed filters. I read attempt-02 in full and confirmed its logic is correct. For the others I only grepped for structure and did not read them in full, and I did not view the screenshots. The differences are minor. Attempts 01 and 02 use var inside an IIFE, while 03–06 use const. Id generation varies between crypto.randomUUID with a fallback and Date.now plus Math.random. Backgrounds are purple gradients in 01, 02, 04 and 05, with a different shade in 01, and a light blue gradient in 06. Attempt 03 appears to have no 'Clear completed' button, and the others do. That is an extra beyond the requirements. All six meet the requirements at comparable quality.

All six use the same basic single-page approach: render a todo array into the DOM, filter by completion state, and save changes to localStorage. The core features are present across attempts, but quality varies: attempts 01 and 02 use form submission and delegated events, while 03 and 05 use separate click/Enter handlers; attempts 02, 04, and 06 add a Clear completed control that the others omit. Persistence error handling and input validation also differ, and several attempts show visibly corrupted delete-button characters. The approach is consistent, but the implementations and polish are not fully comparable.

All six attempts use the same basic design. Each is a single HTML file with one canvas and dat.gui, and each has Growth, Synapses, Pulses and Visuals folders. All use the required neon palette with the three action buttons, shadowBlur glow, a vignette, scanlines, and recursive branches with synapses and pulses. The screenshots show clear differences in quality and look. Attempts 1 and 2 produce a very dense tangle of cyan and yellow-green branches that fills the canvas (attempt 2 has large magenta synapse clusters). Attempts 3 and 4 give a sparser, more organic network. Attempt 3 has about 490 synapses and a status HUD, and attempt 4 has big glowing yellow neuron somas. Attempts 5 and 6 are thin, sparse, tree-like neurons; attempt 5 has a jagged, noisy look with few synapses. Attempt 6 has a visible grid overlay and has Synapses, Pulses and Visuals collapsed. Control naming and units also vary: attempts 1, 2 and 6 use labels like 'branch growth' and 'branch split', while attempts 3 to 5 use camelCase. Slider ranges differ too, for example pulse speed 0.012 against 120 against 2, and glow 1 against 14. Overall the approach is consistent, but the visual quality and density vary noticeably.

All six attempts produce the same broad kind of single canvas neuron growth simulation, with dat.gui controls, neon colors, branching, synapses, and pulses. Their implementations and results vary noticeably: attempts 1–2 grow branch point arrays, attempts 3–5 use different segment or tip based approaches, and attempt 6 caches finished branches on an offscreen canvas. The screenshots range from dense, tangled networks (1–3) to sparser networks (4–6); attempt 3 also displays 626 synapses, far more than the stated cap. The common direction is consistent, but the structure and quality are not comparable across attempts.

I judged this from the six screenshots and the task spec only. I did not open the HTML files, because my shell command to compare them was blocked. All six attempts follow the same approach: a single-file cinematic dark and gold page. They share the same elements:
- The "ARTIFACT" navbar with five links and a gold "Get Tickets" pill.
- The Georgia serif headline "Museum Night, Reimagined".
- An eyebrow line reading "ARTIFACT: Museum Night".
- The date, time and place line.
- Pill badges.
- Gold "Get Tickets" and outlined "Save to Calendar" CTAs.
- A scroll indicator.
- A near-black background with subtle burgundy and navy spotlight gradients.

The visual polish is comparable across attempts. The differences are small and stylistic:
- Four heroes are left-aligned and two (attempts 5 and 6) are centred.
- The "Reimagined" line is italic gold in attempts 1–4 and plain ivory in 5–6.
- Attempts 1–3 show the date, time and place as pills with icons, while attempts 4–6 use inline text.
- Attempt 2 adds a framed border and a vertical "WARSZAWA" label.
- Attempts 3 and 6 show a broken-image icon at the top-left, and in all six the hero photo is not visible, so the source.unsplash.com URLs are not loading.

Quality is consistently good. There is no sign of one attempt being broken or far worse than the others.

All six attempts follow the same broad approach: a dark, gold-accented ARTIFACT landing page with a sticky navigation bar, large serif hero text, event details, and ticket/calendar buttons. Quality varies in the presentation and implementation details: attempts 1–4 use a left-aligned hero, while 5–6 center it; screenshots 3 and 6 show a broken hero image, and attempt 5’s screenshot has no visible hero image. The HTML also differs in its element IDs and markup, and the detected image and artist-card counts vary substantially. The shared design direction is consistent, but the results are not comparable enough to score as fully stable.

All six attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with a canvas 30x30 grid (600px) and a start-menu overlay offering the three modes. Each has a game-over overlay and a BFS-style CPU. That core is consistent, and the shots show all six menus load. They differ in details that affect how the game plays. Human controls are inconsistent: attempts 1, 2, 5 and 6 give P1 WASD and P2 arrows; attempt 3 swaps them (P1 arrows, P2 WASD); attempt 4 uses WASD or arrows for P1 and IJKL for P2. Which snake is the CPU also varies, since attempt 4 makes P1 the CPU in CPU vs Human. Score display varies: attempt 1 shows body length in a header above the canvas, while attempt 4 shows score in an in-canvas HUD and on the game-over screen. Restart and menu keys vary too (R or Space, Enter, M). Attempt 1 ends the game when either snake dies, and attempt 4 does the same, and the other attempts were not inspected for this. Attempt 4 uses requestAnimationFrame and Google Fonts, and attempt 1 uses setInterval. Visual style and quality also differ: attempt 4 is the most polished, with eyes, glow and rounded segments; attempt 1 is plain. Overall this is the same structure with variable detail and polish, so 0.5.

All six attempts use a broadly similar single-file, canvas-based two-snake game with a mode menu, keyboard controls, score display, and CPU movement. Their quality varies: attempt-04 has the most elaborate presentation and game-over flow, while attempt-01 and attempt-02 are simpler implementations; attempt-06 redeclares `mode` with `let` in the same scope, causing a syntax error that prevents the game from running. The screenshots also show substantial variation in layout and visual polish, though the overall approach remains consistent.

All six attempts use the same core approach. Each is a single HTML file with a CPU software rasterizer that writes per-pixel interpolated colour into ImageData and calls putImageData. Each uses rotation matrices, perspective projection, backface culling, Lambert lighting per vertex, a moving light, W and P toggles and an FPS readout. Quality and presentation vary noticeably. Attempts 2, 4 and 6 use a z-buffer, while attempt 1 deliberately has none; attempt 4 renders to an offscreen canvas and attempt 6 renders to a separate buffer. Canvas layout differs: 1, 2 and 3 use a fixed 800x600 canvas, and 4, 5 and 6 fill the whole window. The HUD style also differs between attempts. In the screenshots, attempt 1 shows an odd, stretched near-planar shape, probably from vertex-position normals and a camera that is too close. Attempt 2 is mostly black with a single lit corner. Attempt 3 is very dark and low-contrast. Attempt 4 has clean per-face colours with visible shading and no light marker. Attempt 5 shows a clear, wide cube, and attempt 6 is the most polished, with a visible light marker. The result is a consistent approach with variable visual quality and polish.

All six attempts use the same basic approach: a Canvas 2D software renderer with rotating cube geometry, triangle rasterization, lighting, backface culling, W/P controls, and an FPS display. Quality varies noticeably: the cube is tiny in attempt 03, oversized and partly cropped in attempts 04 and 05, and differently framed in the others; the screenshots also show substantial differences in face colors and lighting, with attempts 02 and 03 especially dark. They are consistent in structure but not in visual result.

All five attempts take the same basic approach. Each is a single HTML file with an 800x800 canvas, dat.gui folders (Growth, Synapses, Pulses, Visuals plus a Controls/Actions folder), the neon palette, a vignette and scanlines, and animated branching growth. Quality varies a lot between them, judging from the screenshots (I did not open the HTML files). Attempt 1 is clean: thin cyan and yellow-green branches, small magenta synapses and visible pulses. Attempt 2 is broken or stalled: only a tiny sprout and a blob of magenta synapses, with almost no network. Attempt 3 looks good: glowing branches, synapses and pulse sparks. Attempt 4 has runaway synapse creation, which produces huge magenta blobs that hide the branches, and its GUI folders are collapsed. Attempt 5 has the same runaway-synapse problem, and its pulse speed and brightness defaults (0.02 and 22) look off. The approach is consistent but the results range from good (1, 3) to visibly broken (2, 4, 5).

All five use a single canvas, dat.gui, neon colors, and animated branching-network concepts, so the overall approach is consistent. Results vary sharply: attempt 01 shows a sparse, readable network; attempts 03 and 05 show denser networks; attempt 04 is overwhelmed by glowing magenta connections; and attempt 02 shows only a small central cluster with no visible branching. The shared approach is recognizable, but the large visual and functional differences make the attempts inconsistent in quality.

All four attempts use the same approach. Each is a single-file page with a dark velvet and gold palette, a Georgia serif headline 'Museum Night, Reimagined', a sticky navbar, gold-gradient CTAs and date/time/place badges. The ICS, modal, Escape and IntersectionObserver keywords appear in every file, so the feature set looks equivalent. Visual execution varies, though. Attempts 1 and 2 use rounded pill buttons and badges, and Attempt 2 adds a hero paragraph and a left-aligned layout. Attempt 3 uses square, uppercase, letter-spaced buttons with an 'Edition IV' eyebrow and an italic serif tagline. Attempt 4 uses a centered, minimal hero with plain text metadata instead of badges and a 'Limited Edition' label. Hero spotlight strength and image treatment also differ. The remote hero image does not appear in any screenshot. The counts of those keywords range from 6 to 17 per file, which suggests different amounts of code and polish. I did not test the functionality of each file, so this is a visual and structural comparison only. Overall: consistent approach and similar quality, with noticeable stylistic and detail variance between attempts.

All four attempts use the same single-file, dark-and-gold cinematic landing-page approach and include the main interaction features, including ticket tiers, modals, FAQ behavior, and calendar download logic. Quality and structure vary: the hero layouts differ visibly across screenshots (centered in 01 and 04, left-aligned in 02 and 03), and section counts range from 7 to 8. Artist-card markup also differs, with attempt 04 showing fewer artist-card references than the others. The attempts are recognizably consistent, but not comparable in execution.

I read attempts 01, 03 and 06 in full and viewed their screenshots. I did not open the source of attempts 02, 04 and 05 or view their screenshots. For those three I only compared file sizes (9.9–12.5 KB), and the screenshot sizes fall into two groups, which suggests two visual styles. All three attempts I read take the same approach: one self-contained HTML file with vanilla JS inside an IIFE and a render() function that rebuilds the list. Each has the same state functions (add, toggle, delete, clear completed, setFilter). All three persist todos and the active filter to localStorage under keys like todo_app_items_v1, wrapped in try/catch with validation on load. Add works by button and Enter key. Completed todos get a line-through class. Delete, All/Active/Completed filters, item counts, empty states and a disabled or hidden 'Clear completed' button are present in each. None of the three has a functional gap. The differences are cosmetic: attempt 01 uses a purple gradient background with a gradient header and an 'items left' footer, while 03 and 06 use a plain light background with a white card. Delete is a hover-revealed 'Delete' text button in 03 and a persistent '×' in 01 and 06. 06 uses var instead of const and adds ARIA roles and a mobile media query. Functional completeness and code quality are comparable across the three I read.

All six use the same basic single-file approach: a todo list rendered in JavaScript, with add, checkbox completion, deletion, filters, and localStorage persistence. Quality varies: attempts 02–06 use the `completed` state consistently, while attempt 01 uses `done`; attempt 06 changes storage keys, and attempt 02's filter key is read without a try/catch. The screenshots also show different layouts and styling, from attempt 01’s purple gradient card to the light layouts in attempts 02–04 and 06. The core approach is consistent, but implementation details and presentation vary across attempts.

The four attempts diverge in approach and in quality. Approach: A1 is a scanline rasterizer drawing flat spans with fillRect on a fixed 480px canvas with a styled DOM HUD. A2 draws every pixel with fillRect on a fullscreen canvas with a canvas-drawn HUD and per-face colours. A3 is a barycentric rasterizer using getImageData/putImageData per triangle, with a light marker. A4 is a barycentric rasterizer with a Z-buffer, a full-frame pixel buffer and a DOM HUD. Camera and culling conventions also differ: A1 looks down +Z, A2 and A3 use normal.z<0 or >0 tests with different signs, and A4 has its own convention. Lighting differs too: A1 uses a single base colour, A2 uses six face colours, A3 uses a single blue with attenuation, and A4 uses six face colours but computes the vertex normal wrongly as normalize(v). Quality varies widely in the screenshots. A1 shows an empty canvas with no cube, so it is broken: the first-frame screenshot has no cube and the code has a centroid bug and a possible culling error. A2 shows a cube with only 3 faces visible, one of them very dark, at 9.4 FPS. A3 shows a single dark, flat-looking polygon that is not a recognisable cube, so its culling or shading is wrong. A4 shows a recognisable cube with several faces, a smooth gradient and 60 FPS. The outputs range from broken to working, so the results are not consistent.

All four use a self-contained Canvas 2D cube renderer with rotation, projection, lighting, and keyboard controls, but the results vary substantially. Attempt 01 shows no cube, and attempt 03 shows only a dark face with a detached light marker. Attempts 02 and 04 render visible rotating cubes, though their colors are mostly flat rather than smoothly Gouraud-shaded; attempt 02 also uses a distinct per-face color palette. The shared general approach is consistent, but functionality and visual quality are not.
